Risk factors for onset Statement • Risk factors for the onset of fecal incontinence include physical conditions, such as age and gender; comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus and IBS; and obstetric conditions, such as the number of deliveries, home delivery, first delivery, and forceps delivery. Commentary Risk factors for the onset of fecal incontinence (FI) include physical conditions, comorbidities, and obstetric conditions. Among physical conditions, age is a clear risk factor for FI, and the majority of epidemiological studies, including young adults, have suggested a clear association between age and FI[ , , , - ]. This may be due to an age-related decline in physical abilities, such as muscle strength and cognitive function, as well as an increase in comorbidities, which are risk factors for FI and are described later. Although many reports have indicated that the prevalence of FI is significantly higher in women than in men[ , , , , ], some have shown no difference in the prevalence of FI between men and women[ , , , ], making gender a relatively weak risk factor for FI. Other physical conditions reported as risk factors for FI include obesity (BMI >30)[ , ], poor general health[ , ], and physical disability[ , ]. Other physical conditions reported as risk factors for FI include obesity (BMI >30)[ , ], poor general health[ , ], and physical disability[ , ]. Systemic comorbidities can also be risk factors for FI. Patients with diabetes mellitus have a higher incidence of FI, and there is a relationship between the degree of blood sugar control and the degree of FI[ ]. Patients with IBS[ ] and inflammatory bowel disease have a high prevalence of FI[ ]. Constipation is the most common cause of FI among children[ ]. Urinary incontinence[ , ], overactive bladder[ ], and pelvic organ prolapse[ , ] are also associated with FI. Dementia[ ] and spinal cord injury[ ] have also been reported as risk factors for FI. Obstetric conditions, such as the number of deliveries[ , ], home delivery[ ], First vaginal delivery[ , ], and forceps delivery[ ], have been reported as risk factors for FI. In addition, fetal size (weight >4,000 g)[ , ] and prolonged second stage of labor[ ] may also be risk factors for gas and FI. The presence of rectal cancer itself may also be a cause of FI, but the rate of LARS, a defecation disorder following anus-preserving surgery for rectal cancer, is as high as 80%-90%[ ], and the number of patients living with defecation disorder even after radical cure continues to increase every year. II. Diagnosis and Evaluation of Fecal Incontinence A. Initial clinical assessment of fecal incontinence The initial clinical assessment of fecal incontinence (FI) involves evaluation of its severity and impact on QoL as well as identification of its causes based on medical history, symptoms of FI, and physical examination of the anorectal area. In addition, examinations, such as colonoscopy, are performed as necessary to identify organic diseases, such as ulcerative colitis, that may cause FI. This initial clinical assessment is fundamental for the management of FI, as it is necessary to differentiate FI caused by organic diseases, such as rectal prolapse, and to select appropriate initial conservative therapies. 1. Medical history, observation, and assessment Statement • It is recommended to take medical history, including symptoms of fecal incontinence, and to observe and assess the patient's cognitive and motor functions, as they are useful for evaluating the severity of fecal incontinence and its impact on quality of life, as well as for identifying the cause. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: D Abstract The symptoms of fecal incontinence (FI) are classified as urge FI, passive FI, and mixed FI, in which both coexist, and stool consistency is evaluated using the Bristol Stool Form Scale. Because FI is often caused by multiple factors, medical history should be taken considering various pathological conditions, causes, and risk factors. History of the present disease should focus on details related to FI, such as its onset and severity, and on daily bowel habits and activities related to FI. In addition, patients' past medical history, obstetric history, and comorbidities associated with FI should be reviewed. Because cognitive and motor dysfunctions can also cause FI, the observation and assessment of cognitive and motor functions are important for the treatment and care of FI. A bowel diary is useful for assessing the occurrence and factors of FI and for managing oral medications. Commentary a. History of present illness The symptoms of FI are classified as urge FI, passive FI, and mixed FI, in which both coexist[ ]. Urge FI is “a symptom of feeling the urge to defecate but passing feces without being able to hold it until one reaches the toilet,” while passive FI is “a symptom of not feeling the urge to defecate and passing feces without realizing it.” FI is rarely caused by a single factor and is often the result of multiple interrelated causes[ ]. In other words, FI is caused by factors such as abnormal stool consistency, decreased anal pressure, impaired rectoanal sensation, defecation disorder, abnormal rectal capacity, pressure or compliance, colon dysfunction, and cognitive or motor dysfunction, occurring alone or in combination (see “I-C. Pathophysiology and Causes”). When anal sphincter dysfunction is the main cause of FI, a decrease in internal anal sphincter function is likely to cause passive FI due to a decrease in resting anal canal pressure, whereas a decrease in external anal sphincter function may cause urge FI due to decreased anal canal voluntary contraction pressure[ ]. Pathophysiology and Causes”). When anal sphincter dysfunction is the main cause of FI, a decrease in internal anal sphincter function is likely to cause passive FI due to a decrease in resting anal canal pressure, whereas a decrease in external anal sphincter function may cause urge FI due to decreased anal canal voluntary contraction pressure[ ]. In contrast, even if the anal sphincters are perfectly normal, if rectal sensation is decreased and the patient does not feel the urge to defecate even when there are feces in the rectum, fecal impaction may occur, resulting in overflow passive FI. Furthermore, patients with IBS, in whom rectal sensation and contractility are increased, may experience urge FI even when the anal sphincters are perfectly normal because the strong rectal contractions that occur as a defecation reflex in response to hypersensitivity to the urge to defecate cause the feces in the rectum to be expelled. In a survey of 472 patients with IBS living in the United States and Sweden, nearly 20% had FI on at least 1 day per month[ ]. Another theory is that passive FI occurs when feces remaining in the rectum leak after defecation because they cannot be completely evacuated during defecation due to rectal intussusception or rectocele or because the rectal wall invaginates into the rectal lumen, inducing the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, resulting in decreased resting anal canal pressure[ ]. During the interview, medical history should be collected regarding the patient's daily bowel habits and FI, focusing on the risk factors for FI while considering the various pathological conditions described above. For this purpose, a detailed bowel movement record and description of the patient's daily life, including dietary habits, are recommended[ , , ]. Although medical history alone may not provide an accurate estimate of the pathophysiology or cause of FI, it may help determine the need for treatment and further examination, including specialized examinations. 1) Questions regarding daily bowel habits • What were your bowel movements like before the onset of FI? • When and how did they change? • Are you using medications such as laxatives, enemas, irrigation, or suppositories? Since when and to what extent? • How often do you normally have bowel movements? • What is your usual stool form? (Described based on the Bristol Stool Form Scale) ( ) • Do you usually have a roughly fixed time for bowel movement? (Regular or irregular?) • Do you strain excessively when defecating? If you strain, to what extent and for how long? • Can you distinguish between stool and gas? Can you distinguish between liquid and solid stool? • Do you feel abdominal pain or bloating before defecation? • Do you need assistance with using a finger or hand to defecate? • Can you wipe yourself clean after defecation? • How active are you in your daily life? 2) Questions on FI • When did the first episode of FI occur? How has it changed over time since then? • Was there a trigger that caused FI? • Can you perceive if you have fecal leakage? Are you experiencing consciously uncontrolled fecal continence? • Is there leakage of gas, mucus, liquid stool, or solid stool? How often, how much, and what is the stool form? • Can you hold your bowel movements? How long can you hold them? • Can you hold your flatus? How long can you hold it? • Do you have stool leakage after defecation? • Do you have stool leakage during sleep? • Does FI interfere with your daily activities? If yes, what kind of effects, how often, and to what extent? • Are you using hygiene products, such as pads? If yes, how often and how many pieces? 3) Questions about daily life related to FI • Dietary intake, indulgences (coffee, alcohol, etc.), and fluid intake • Smoking history and changes in body weight (BMI) • Oral medications such as laxatives and psychotropic drugs • Daily routine (waking up, eating, going to school/working, bedtime, etc.) • Living environment, including toilets (accessibility to toilets, use of warm-water bidet and toilet seat, and Japanese-style or Western-style toilets) • Pain caused by defecation posture or difficulty maintaining defecation posture (joint contracture, etc.) Stool consistency is one of factors affecting FI[ ], and diarrhea can cause urge FI. In contrast, chronic constipation, such as rectal fecal impaction, caused by rectal hyposensitivity, can cause passive FI. Because defecation status, including FI, varies greatly by person, it is necessary to confirm the daily bowel habits of each patient and assess the changes in these habits. It is preferable to evaluate and describe stool consistency using the internationally used Bristol Stool Form Scale

In contrast, chronic constipation, such as rectal fecal impaction, caused by rectal hyposensitivity, can cause passive FI. Because defecation status, including FI, varies greatly by person, it is necessary to confirm the daily bowel habits of each patient and assess the changes in these habits. It is preferable to evaluate and describe stool consistency using the internationally used Bristol Stool Form Scale ( )[ ]. However, it must be used with the understanding that there may not be perfect agreement among the evaluators. In particular, it is difficult to distinguish between types 2 and 3 and types 5 and 6[ ]. When interviewing about symptoms of FI, the degree and time course of FI should be evaluated, considering the pathophysiology, causes, and risk factors of FI. In addition, the living environment, including the toilet environment, and the patient's general condition, including movement restriction, cognitive ability, and level of activities of daily living[ ], should be evaluated as factors related to the manifestation of FI symptoms in daily life. Because diarrhea caused by regular medications for comorbidities may be involved in the onset of FI, the patient's medications should be reviewed in detail. Inappropriate use of laxatives for constipation often causes FI. Psychotropic drugs may cause FI by affecting intestinal motility and peripheral nerves[ ]. Indulgences, such as coffee and alcohol, can cause urge FI by affecting intestinal motility and stool consistency[ ]. Furthermore, because obesity is a risk factor for FI, changes in body weight should also be monitored[ ]. As described above, FI is often caused by multiple factors; thus, it is necessary to take medical history considering various pathological conditions, causes, and risk factors. Taking a history of present illness, including symptoms of FI, is useful for evaluating the severity of FI and its impact on quality of life and for identifying the causes of FI. The European guideline[ ] and the ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ] also “strongly recommend” that “the cause of FI should be identified based on medical history” as an expert opinion. b. History and comorbidities The following diseases and physical conditions are factors associated with FI, as well as history and comorbidities that may be risk factors for FI (see “I-C. Pathophysiology and Causes”). • Diseases and physical conditions that affect intestinal motility • Diarrhea, constipation, enteritis, IBS, diabetes mellitus, history of cholecystectomy, etc. • Diseases and physical conditions that affect rectoanal sensory function • IBS, vaginal delivery (pudendal neuropathy due to overextension of nerves), spinal nerve disease or injury, chronic constipation, anal malformation and its history, diabetes mellitus, dementia, etc. • Diseases and physical conditions that affect anal sphincter function • Vaginal delivery (anal sphincter injury due to perineal lacerations or pudendal neuropathy due to overextension of nerves), anal surgery or trauma, spinal nerve disease or injury, aging, etc. • Diseases and physical conditions that affect rectal capacity and extensibility • History of intrapelvic surgery, such as in the rectum or uterus, IBS, history of radiation therapy, inflammatory bowel disease, constipation (chronic distension of the rectum), rectal and anal cancer, etc. • Diseases and physical conditions that reduce stool evacuation performance • Movement restriction due to cerebral infarction, age-related generalized muscle weakness, dementia, etc. • Other diseases and physical conditions that may cause FI • Actions and side effects of oral medications (laxatives, etc.), hemorrhoids, anal fistula, rectal prolapse, rectal intussusception, inflammation of the rectum and perineum, rectal fecal impaction, etc. 1) Obstetric history For obstetric history, in addition to the presence or absence of a history of childbirth, confirm the mode of delivery (vaginal or cesarean section), whether using forceps or vacuum, the number of deliveries, the degree of perineal laceration, the birth weight of the infant, and postpartum defecation status. Obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS) are an important cause of FI in women. According to a study that used endoanal ultrasound for evaluation, the incidence of OASIS is 27%-35% in primiparas[ ]; however, its occurrence does not necessarily indicate the development of anal incontinence (including gas incontinence). In a prospective study by Sultan et al.[ ] who evaluated 79 primiparas before and after vaginal delivery using endoanal ultrasonography, OASIS occurred in 28 primiparas (35%) after vaginal delivery; however, among them, only about one-third, or 10 primiparas (13%), developed anal incontinence or fecal urgency. Anal incontinence developed in 1.2% of women after vaginal delivery, even if OASIS did not occur; thus, it is necessary to consider anal sphincter injury and pudendal neuropathy during delivery as the cause of anal incontinence after delivery[ ]. In a prospective study by Sultan et al.[ ] who evaluated 79 primiparas before and after vaginal delivery using endoanal ultrasonography, OASIS occurred in 28 primiparas (35%) after vaginal delivery; however, among them, only about one-third, or 10 primiparas (13%), developed anal incontinence or fecal urgency. Anal incontinence developed in 1.2% of women after vaginal delivery, even if OASIS did not occur; thus, it is necessary to consider anal sphincter injury and pudendal neuropathy during delivery as the cause of anal incontinence after delivery[ ]. Risk factors for the onset of anal incontinence after vaginal delivery include third- or fourth-degree perineal laceration (anal sphincter injury), forceps or vacuum delivery, maternal obesity, and advanced age[ , - ]. 2) History of surgery and radiation therapy A history of hysterectomy, anal surgery, rectal surgery, and other surgeries, such as cholecystectomy, as well as a history of radiation therapy to the pelvic region, may cause FI. FI caused by anal surgery (for anal fissure, anal fistula, hemorrhoids, etc.) is attributed to direct surgical manipulation of the anal sphincters and anal sphincter injury resulting from hyperextension of the anal canal during surgery[ ]. In LARS, a defecation disorder after rectal resection[ ], or after total colectomy and ileoanal anastomosis for ulcerative colitis, FI can occur. This may be due to decreased fecal retention capacity following colon or rectal resection and decreased anal sphincter function, and changes in stool consistency and the sensation of stool retention. Hysterectomy also causes urinary and FI[ ]. In addition, surgery for prostate cancer or rectal and anal cancer may be combined with radiation therapy, which further increases the risk of FI[ , ]. In addition to surgery in the anus or pelvic cavity, diarrhea after cholecystectomy is a risk factor for FI[ ]. 3) Spinal or spinal cord diseases and a history of pelvic trauma Spinal or spinal cord diseases (spinal cord injury, spina bifida, spinal canal stenosis, etc.), history of spinal or spinal cord surgery, and history of pelvic and sacroiliac trauma directly affect the sensory and motor nerves distributed in the pelvic floor. In addition, diarrhea and constipation caused by autonomic neuropathy mediated by spinal nerves can cause FI[ , - ]. 4) Diabetes mellitus Diabetes mellitus is recognized as a risk factor for FI because it is accompanied by systemic peripheral neuropathy and impairs intestinal motility and sensory nerves of the rectum and motor nerves of the anal sphincters[ , , ]. In a survey of 8,657 participants, symptoms of FI were correlated with blood glucose control[ ]. 5) Neuromuscular disease In neuromuscular diseases such as Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, lateral sclerosis, and scleroderma, autonomic and motor nerves are systemically impaired, whereas peripheral neuropathy occurs in the rectum, anal sphincter, and pelvic floor muscles[ ]. Rectal capacity, sensation, and extensibility are decreased, and the contractility of the anal sphincters is also decreased, causing FI[ , ]. In contrast, when the central nervous system is impaired because of cerebral infarction or other causes, FI is often caused by impaired rectoanal function, cognitive decline, and decreased motor functions, such as mobility and movement restrictions[ , ]. 6) Urinary incontinence Urinary and FI have common pathogenesis resulting from impaired pelvic floor muscles and nerves. The prevalence of postpartum urinary and FI is 6%-8%, but the incidence is higher in primiparas over 35 years of age who undergo forceps or suction delivery[ , , ]. About one-third of female patients with urinary incontinence who gave birth experience FI, which is a higher complication rate than that among men[ ]. The onset of urinary and FI is correlated with depression (odds ratio 2.3), indicating that psychological factors are involved in the onset of incontinence. 7) Diseases causing abnormal stool consistency, such as constipation and diarrhea Chronic enteritis, IBS[ , ], and diseases that cause abnormal stool consistency, such as constipation and diarrhea, are risk factors for FI[ , ]. IBS, in particular, has a high odds ratio of 2.4 for the onset of FI and is considered a clear risk factor[ ]. c. Anorectal examination and evaluation Visual inspection (including anoscopy and proctoscopy) and palpation (including digital anorectal and vaginal examination) of the anorectal area, focusing on factors associated with the onset of fecal incontinence, should be conducted, following medical history taking and general physical and anal examinations. a. Visual inspection Statement ・Visual inspection is recommended because it is useful for evaluating the pathophysiology of fecal incontinence and identifying its causes. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: D Abstract Visual inspection is useful for evaluating the pathophysiology of fecal incontinence (FI) and identifying its causes by observing the external appearance of the anus at rest, including its shape, the condition of the surrounding skin, the presence or absence of scars, and the movement of the anus and perineum during contraction of the anal sphincter and straining. It is also useful for evaluating the state of FI and identifying the cause. Commentary Although no studies have directly evaluated the usefulness of visual inspection in the management of FI, a physical examination of the anorectal area, including visual inspection, is “strongly recommended” as an expert opinion in the European guideline[ ] and is summarized as “an essential component of the evaluation of patients with FI” in the American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ]. At rest, check the symmetry of the anus and perineum; presence of stool, mucus, or blood on the area; and presence or absence and extent of anal or perineal scars (position, size, and shape) from anal surgery, perineal lacerations, or episiotomy as well as superficial skin lesions (dermatitis, flare reaction, avulsion, and maceration)[ , - ]. In addition, observe the condition of anal closure and the presence or absence of visible anal lesions, such as rectal prolapse, mucosal prolapse, and hemorrhoids. In women, confirm the distance between the vaginal orifice and the anus and perform a visual inspection with attention to the direction of the scars caused by episiotomy, as the risk of anal sphincter injury is reported to be higher with a midline episiotomy than with a mediolateral episiotomy during vaginal delivery[ , ]. During anal sphincter contraction, observe whether the closure of the anus with contraction is circumferential and uniform and whether indentations or retractions appear due to anal sphincter defects. During straining, observe the descent of the anus and perineum. Excessive perineal descent suggests that the pelvic floor muscles are flaccid, which can cause FI[ ]. Visual inspection using an anoscope or proctoscope is useful for the diagnosis of organic abnormalities that may cause FI, such as anorectal tumors, hemorrhoids, rectal ulcers, and scars from anal surgery (hemorrhoidectomy, fistula surgery,

During straining, observe the descent of the anus and perineum. Excessive perineal descent suggests that the pelvic floor muscles are flaccid, which can cause FI[ ]. Palpation 1) Palpation of perianal area Statement ・Palpation is recommended to evaluate the sensation of the perianal skin in patients with suspected anorectal hyposensitivity. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: D Abstract Evaluation of perianal skin sensation by palpation and assessment of anal sphincter defects by perianal skin compression are useful for identifying the causes of fecal incontinence (FI) in patients with suspected anorectal hyposensitivity. Commentary Although no studies have directly evaluated the usefulness of palpation in the management of FI, a physical examination of the anorectal area, including palpation, is “strongly recommended” as an expert opinion in the European guideline[ ] and is summarized as “an essential component of the evaluation of patients with FI” in the American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ]. In patients with suspected anorectal hyposensitivity, such as those with spinal cord impairment and older adults, evaluate perianal skin sensation by palpation. Evaluation of perianal skin sensation is particularly important in patients presenting with rectal fecal impaction, as rectal sensation is often decreased. Evaluation of perianal skin sensation is easier when compared with other body parts with apparently normal sensations. The areas of neuropathy that can be diagnosed by palpation according to the area of distribution from the spinal nerves to the skin sensory nerves are S3: outer perianal area, and S4-5: perianal area[ , ]. Therefore, when perianal skin sensation has decreased, S3-5 sacral neuropathy is suspected. In addition, if S2-4 sacral nerves are intact, an anocutaneous reflex, called “anal wink”, is present, in which the external anal sphincter contracts when the perianal skin is stimulated with a needle[ ]; however, this reflex is not observed in S2-4 sacral neuropathy. It is useful for identifying significant anal sphincter injury to evaluate subcutaneous anal sphincter defects with resistance to light pressure on the perianal skin by palpation with fingers. However, failure to identify an abnormality by palpation does not necessarily mean that an anal sphincter defect does not exist because minor defects cannot be identified with such a palpation. In women, palpation of tissue integrity in the perineum between the anus and vagina is useful for assessing the consequences of perineal lacerations during vaginal delivery. 2) Digital anorectal examination (including digital vaginal and bidigital examinations) Statement ・Digital anorectal examination is recommended to be performed because it is useful for evaluating the pathophysiology of fecal incontinence and identifying its causes. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B Abstract Digital anorectal examination is useful for evaluating the pathophysiology of fecal incontinence (FI) and identifying its causes by assessing rectal tumors and masses, rectal fecal impaction, rectocele, anal canal tone, voluntary contraction pressure, anal canal deformity and asymmetry, as well as the presence or absence and degree of pelvic floor incoordination. Commentary Several studies have examined the usefulness of digital anorectal examination for the treatment of FI compared with anal manometry and endoanal ultrasonography[ , - ], although no RCTs have investigated it. The European guideline[ ] “strongly recommends” as an expert opinion that “Inspection and physical examination of the anorectal region should be performed to assess anorectal pathology and/or fecal impaction and to evaluate anal state/tone at rest and during voluntary effort”. In addition, digital anorectal examination is summarized as “an essential component of the evaluation of patients with FI” in the American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ] and is recommended with “Grade of Recommendation B” by the 6th International Consultation on Incontinence[ ]. When a mass that seems to be a tumor is palpated in the rectum by digital rectal examination, colonoscopy is necessary to diagnose and differentiate organic diseases such as rectal cancer. If a significant amount of fecal mass is palpated in the rectum, passive FI due to the mechanism of overflow FI associated with rectal fecal impaction is very likely[ ]. After removal of the fecal mass, therefore, periodic rectal emptying should be performed with scheduled defecation regimens and bowel habit instructions. In addition, anorectal physiology tests should be considered to evaluate rectal sensation because it may be decreased in patients with fecal impaction. If a rectocele is found

If a significant amount of fecal mass is palpated in the rectum, passive FI due to the mechanism of overflow FI associated with rectal fecal impaction is very likely[ ]. After removal of the fecal mass, therefore, periodic rectal emptying should be performed with scheduled defecation regimens and bowel habit instructions. In addition, anorectal physiology tests should be considered to evaluate rectal sensation because it may be decreased in patients with fecal impaction. If a rectocele is found in women, consider performing defecography, as residual stool in the rectum due to structural evacuation disorders, such as rectocele, may be the cause of post-defecation passive FI[ ]. Digital anal examination is useful for evaluating the contractility of the anal sphincter, and when performed by an experienced examiner, the contractility of the internal and external anal sphincters and the puborectal muscle can be evaluated fairly accurately[ ]. This is based on the fact that several studies have reported a high correlation between anal canal tone and voluntary contraction pressure evaluated by digital anal examination and maximum resting pressure and maximum voluntary contraction pressure evaluated by anal manometry, respectively[ , - ]. In particular, Orkin et al.[ ] developed the Digital Rectal Examination Scoring System (DRESS; ), which evaluates resting pressure and squeeze pressure on a six-point scale (DRESS score) from 0 to 5 as a subjective evaluation method of anal canal tone and voluntary contraction pressure by digital anal examination. In 303 patients with defecatory concerns, each DRESS score was compared with the results of anal manometry. The resting DRESS score showed a good correlation with mean maximum resting pressure by anal manometry with resting DRESS scores of 0: 21 mmHg, 1: 39 mmHg, 2: 48 mmHg, 3: 72 mmHg, 4: 94 mmHg, and 5: 128 mmHg (correlation coefficient: 0.82). In addition, the squeeze DRESS score showed a good correlation with mean maximum voluntary contraction pressure by anal manometry with squeeze DRESS scores of 0: 46 mmHg, 1: 67 mmHg, 2: 108 mmHg, 3: 156 mmHg, 4: 239 mmHg, and 5: 368 mmHg (correlation coefficient: 0.81). Digital anal examination for the evaluation of anal canal deformity and asymmetry has low diagnostic accuracy for mild anal sphincter defects and disruptions, but is useful for the diagnosis of severe defects and disruptions[ , , ]. Dobben et al.[ ] compared the diagnosis of external anal sphincter defects by digital anal examination with that by endoanal ultrasonography in 312 patients with FI. Their study revealed an agreement rate of 100% for severe defects of 150°-270° by endoanal ultrasonography but a low agreement rate of 61% for defects of 90°-150° and 36% for defects of less than 90°. In addition, Jeppson et al.[ ] examined the diagnostic accuracy of anal sphincter disruptions by digital anal examination in 74 patients with FI based on the diagnosis of anal sphincter disruptions by endoanal ultrasonography. The sensitivity of digital anal examination was demonstrated to be high (82%), whereas the specificity was low (32%). Therefore, when the diagnosis of the anal sphincter disruptions is made by digital anal examination, it is relatively reliable, and at the same time, the disruptions are likely to be severe. In contrast, when a diagnosis of no anal sphincter disruption is made by digital anal examination, it is less reliable, and it is possible that minor disruptions may be overlooked. When the patient is asked to strain as if defecating during digital anorectal examination, and pelvic floor incoordination is detected, in which the puborectal muscle and external anal sphincter contract without the ability to remain relaxed, this may indicate a functional defecation disorder. If residual stool in the rectum due to functional defecation disorder is suspected of causing post-defecation passive FI, consider performing a defecography or rectal balloon expulsion test[ ]. The diagnostic accuracy of pelvic floor incoordination by digital anorectal examination is relatively high, with a reported sensitivity of 75%-93% and specificity of 59%-87% compared with diagnosis by anal manometry or balloon expulsion test[ , ]. Digital vaginal and bidigital examinations are performed in the same manner as digital anorectal examinations. Digital vaginal examination can evaluate the fragility of the rectovaginal septum and the presence or absence of uterine or bladder descent caused by abdominal pressure. In addition, enterocele and sigmoidocele can be diagnosed via bidigital examination of the rectum and vagina[ ]. As described above, digital anorectal examination is useful for evaluating the pathophysiology of FI and planning its management. In a survey by Wong et al.[ ] of 652 gastroenterologists, medical practitioners, and medical students, the rates of performing digital anorectal examination for patients with FI were 100% among gastroenterologists, 83% among medical practitioners, and 79% among medical students. Evaluation of incontinence-associated dermatitis Statement • To provide care and treatment appropriate to the cause, the evaluation of the causes and risk factors of incontinence-associated dermatitis is proposed to be performed by categorizing them into systemic (skin fragility) and local factors (buttock and perineum environment). Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 90.9%), Level of Evidence: D Abstract Incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) is caused by contact of the skin with excrement, such as urine and feces. IAD causes unbearable pain, itching, and secondary infections, requiring appropriate prevention, care, and treatment. In the assessment of IAD, risk factors are evaluated by dividing them into systemic factors (skin fragility) and local factors (buttock and perineum environment). In addition, it is useful to evaluate its severity by scoring using the IAD Severity Evaluation Scale. Commentary IAD is caused by contact of the skin with excrement, such as urine and feces. The prevalence of IAD varies depending on the survey participant and facility and is 7.6%-45.7%[ - ] in Europe and the United States and 5.9%-17%[ , ] among residents of long-term care health facilities in Japan. IAD causes unbearable pain, itching, and secondary infections, requiring appropriate prevention, care, and treatment. When stool comes in contact with the skin because of incontinence, the moisture in the stool causes swelling of keratinocytes and expansion of the interstitial spaces between corneocytes, resulting in skin maceration. In addition, digestive enzymes in the stool damage the stratum corneum and allow irritants to pass through the skin barrier, thereby causing inflammation. The effects are particularly severe in the case of liquid or soft stools[ ]. Furthermore, when diapers or pads are used for incontinence, the skin becomes excessively moist in the hot and humid environment, compromising the skin barrier function. As a result, bacteria and fungi invade the skin, causing epidermal defects, erosions, exudation, vesicle formation, edema, and redness. 1) Assessment of IAD[<xref rid="B122" ref-type="bibr">122</xref>-<xref rid="B128" ref-type="bibr">128</xref>] The causes and risk factors are evaluated in the following two categories: 1 Systemic factors (skin fragility) • Malnutrition • Aging • Diabetes mellitus with poor blood glucose control • Use of immunosuppressants • Use of anticancer drugs • Use of steroids • Use of antibiotics • Dry skin 2 Local factors (buttock and perineum environment) • Liquid or soft stool • Coexistence of fecal and urinary incontinence • Use of diapers, pads, etc. • Maceration due to excrement • Pressure or misalignment due to maintaining the same position, such as head elevation or sitting • Improper skin care (excessive washing and wiping) 2) IAD severity evaluation scale (IAD-set) The IAD-set, a tool developed to assess IAD in clinical settings in Japan, evaluates and scores two items, namely “I. Skin condition” and “II. The type of excrement attached.” “I. Skin condition” is scored for the degree of skin damage and the suspicion of candidiasis in each of the eight sites on the buttocks. “II. The type of excrement attached” is scored based on the characteristics of the attached feces and urine, and the total score is obtained by adding I and II together[ ]. The reliability of this scale developed in Japan has been confirmed, and it allows quantitative evaluation. However, effective use requires training due to a large number of observational items and the possibility of confusion in judging skin condition. Therefore, currently, this scale is not widely used in clinical settings; however, further evaluation of its usefulness in clinical practice is expected in the future. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 90%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract For the clinical evaluation of fecal incontinence (FI), it is useful to use Patient-Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs), such as scores and questionnaires, to evaluate the symptomatic severity of FI and its impact on QoL. The CCFIS comprises five questions and is suitable for daily clinical practice because it allows the simultaneous evaluation of the symptomatic severity of anal incontinence (AI) and QoL. The St. Mark's Score comprises seven questions and is also suitable for daily clinical practice with an emphasis on fecal urgency because it allows the evaluation of fecal urgency in addition to five items in the CCFIS. The FISI comprises four questions and is unique in that it evaluates only the symptomatic severity of AI, with each symptom assigned a weighted score. However, because it cannot evaluate QoL, FI-specific QoL evaluation scales, such as the Fecal Incontinence Quality of Life Scale (FIQL), should be used concurrently when the FISI is used for the clinical evaluation of FI. Objective evaluation scales allow the comparison of FI severity among different populations and the evaluation of improvement with treatment. The ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ] recommend, with a low level of evidence, that scores and questionnaires that evaluate the severity of FI and its impact on QoL should be used depending on the situation. There are many scales for evaluating the severity of FI, including the CCFIS[ ], St. Mark's Score[ ], FISI[ ], and Kirwan classification[ ]. In addition, the Initial Measurement of Patient-Reported Pelvic Floor Complaints Tool (IMPACT) was developed to comprehensively evaluate FI as well as constipation, urinary incontinence, symptoms of pelvic organ prolapse, and symptoms of pelvic floor dysfunction, such as sexual dysfunction. IMPACT-B (Bowel function), a part of the IMPACT, is used to evaluate the symptoms of defecation disorders, including FI[ ]. Among these, the CCFIS ( ), St. Mark's Score ( ), and FISI ( ) are commonly used to evaluate the symptomatic severity of FI[ ]. The CCFIS was previously called the Wexner Score but is now commonly referred to as the Cleveland Clinic Florida FI Score after the institution, rather than the individual, that developed it[ ]. The CCFIS consists of a total of five items, including three items addressing the form (gas, liquid stool, or solid stool) and their frequency of incontinence, as well as two items addressing the frequency of “the use of pads to prevent underwear soiling” and “the impact of FI on daily life,” with the total score ranging from 0 (no FI) to 20 (most severe FI). Because it includes the evaluation of gas incontinence, it should actually be referred to as an anal incontinence score, but it is customary to refer to it as a FI score, in addition to the St. Mark's Score and FISI, although they include gas incontinence as an evaluation item. The advantages of the CCFIS are that it is a relatively simple five-item instrument that allows the simultaneous evaluation of FI symptoms and QoL components, such as the impact on daily life, and that it is widely used historically and internationally. Therefore, from the viewpoint of simplicity, the CCFIS is recommended for evaluating the symptomatic severity of FI and its impact on QoL in daily clinical practice. In contrast, the disadvantages of the CCFIS are that it does not assign weighting to the symptoms to be evaluated, such that 4 points are assigned to daily leakage, regardless of whether the patient leaks solid stool or gas, and that the score itself does not necessarily reflect the symptoms of FI alone, as it evaluates FI symptoms and QoL simultaneously. In other words, similar to how FI is called a “symptom of anxiety,” even if the FI symptoms have been completely cured by treatment, some patients may continue to use pads and their daily lives may continue to be affected until their anxiety regarding FI is resolved. Thus, their CCFIS can remain at a maximum score of 8. Another disadvantage of the CCFIS is that it cannot evaluate fecal urgency, which can be a major concern for some patients, even if it does not actually lead to FI. A study comparing the CCFIS and QoL found that patients with a CCFIS >9 had significantly more impaired QoL than those with a CCFIS ≤9[ ]. The study recommends achieving a CCFIS ≤9 in clinical practice. In addition, a study that evaluated clinically significant minimally important differences (MID)[ ] in FI severity evaluation scales has found that the MID for the CCFIS is 2 to 3 points[ ]. For example, in a clinical study, even if a treatment method improves the CCFIS from 12 to 10.5 points, which is a statistically significant difference, an improvement of 1.5 points is not a clinically significant improvement, as it has not reached the MID of 2 to 3 points. In clinical practice, a CCFIS improvement of at least 3 points can be considered a reasonable target. The St. Mark's Score, also called the Vaizey Score, consists of a total of seven items, including the two items of “presence or absence of fecal urgency” and “presence or absence of antidiarrheal use,” in addition to the five items in the CCFIS, with the total score ranging from 0 (no FI) to 24 (most severe FI)[ ]. The advantage of the St. Mark's Score is that it can also evaluate fecal urgency in addition to the evaluation items in the CCFIS. Therefore, St. Mark's Score is recommended for evaluating the symptomatic severity of FI and its impact on QoL in daily clinical practice with an emphasis on fecal urgency. In contrast, the disadvantages of St. Mark's Score are, that similar to the CCFIS, it does not assign weighting to

absence of antidiarrheal use,” in addition to the five items in the CCFIS, with the total score ranging from 0 (no FI) to 24 (most severe FI)[ ]. The advantage of the St. Mark's Score is that it can also evaluate fecal urgency in addition to the evaluation items in the CCFIS. Therefore, St. Mark's Score is recommended for evaluating the symptomatic severity of FI and its impact on QoL in daily clinical practice with an emphasis on fecal urgency. In contrast, the disadvantages of St. Mark's Score are, that similar to the CCFIS, it does not assign weighting to the symptoms to be evaluated, and that the score itself does not necessarily reflect the symptomatic severity of FI, as it evaluates FI symptoms and QoL simultaneously. The MID for St. Mark's Score is reported as 3-5 points[ ]. Therefore, in clinical practice, an improvement of at least 5 points in the St. Mark's Score can be considered a reasonable target. The FISI consists of four items addressing the form (gas, mucus, liquid stool, or solid stool) and its frequency of incontinence, with the total score ranging from 0 (no FI) to 61 (most severe FI)[ ]. The advantages of FISI are that, unlike CCFIS and St. Mark's Score, it evaluates symptoms only and assigns weighting to the symptoms to be evaluated. However, its advantage of “evaluating only symptoms” may also be disadvantageous because it “can only evaluate symptoms.” Therefore, when the FISI is used for the clinical evaluation of FI, a FI-specific QoL evaluation scale should be used concurrently because the goal of management for FI is to improve the patient's QoL by alleviating symptoms. FI-specific QoL evaluation scales include the FIQL[ ] and Modified Manchester Health Questionnaire[ ]. In addition, the International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire (ICIQ) was developed to comprehensively evaluate QoL related to FI as well as constipation, urinary incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapse; the ICIQ-B (Bowels), which is a part of the ICIQ, is used to evaluate QoL related to defecation disorders, including FI[ ]. Among these, the FIQL is the internationally most widely used FI-specific QoL evaluation scale[ ]. The FIQL consists of 29 questions categorized into four elements, and the scores are expressed as mean scores, with higher scores indicating better QoL)[ ]. The number of questions and the range of scores for each element are as follows: Lifestyle (10 questions, 1-4 points), Coping/Behavior (9 questions, 1-4 points), Depression/Self-perception (7 questions, 1-4.4 points) and Embarrassment (3 questions, 1-4 points). Since its development in the United States, the FIQL has been translated into many languages with verified reliability and validity, including two Japanese versions[ , ]. The Japanese versions allow evaluation of not only each element but also the total score (1-4.1 points). Although FIQL is extremely useful for evaluating FI-specific QoL, the number of questions is too large to be used routinely in daily clinical practice because of their complexity. Therefore, in clinical studies requiring accurate evaluation of QoL, it is recommended to evaluate both the symptomatic severity of FI and FI-specific QoL using the FISI and the Japanese version of the FIQL, respectively, at the same time. Two studies reported that the MID for the FIQL was 1.1 to 1.2 points[ ] and 0.7 to 1.1 points[ ]. Even when the same questionnaire is used, the MID varies depending on the participant and method of investigation[ ]. In LARS, not only FI but also frequent bowel movements within a short period of time called “clustering” are often problematic; thus, the LARS Score[ ], which considers LARS-specific symptoms, is more suitable than CCFIS and FISI as a scale for evaluating symptomatic severity of LARS, and its Japanese version is available with verified reliability and validity ( )[ ]. However, the LARS score evaluates symptoms related to FI, such as gas and liquid FI, fecal urgency, and clustering, but does not evaluate evacuation difficulty and the sensation of incomplete defecation, which are sometimes problematic in LARS. In addition, the impact of LARS on QoL is not evaluated, and some reports have indicated that the LARS score does not reflect the degree of impairment in QoL[ ]. In clinical research, treatment success is commonly defined as a reduction of at least 50% in the mean number of FI episodes per week[ ]. However, according to an online survey, only 58% of patients with FI accepted a reduction of at least 50% in FI frequency as the definition of treatment success, with only 26% of older adults aged ≥65 years accepting it, in particular. While many patients considered a reduction of at least 75% as the definition of treatment success, younger people and patients with severe FI tended to accept a reduction of at least 50% as the definition of treatment success[ ]. Regarding the statement at the beginning, “In clinical studies, treatment success is proposed to be defined as a reduction of at least 50% in the mean number of FI episodes per week after treatment compared with that before treatment,” there were opinions supporting it as a strong recommendation during the vote to determine the strength of recommendation in the Guideline Preparation Committee. III. Examinations for Fecal Incontinence (more detailed description) Examinations for fecal incontinence (FI) are performed to determine its causes and pathophysiology. A comprehensive diagnosis based on symptoms, medical history, physical findings, and the results of multiple tests is often required because it is difficult to determine the cause and pathophysiology accurately with a single examination. These tests include anorectal manometry, anorectal sensation tests, pudendal nerve terminal motor latency (PNTML), anal electromyography, ultrasonography, pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and defecography. These tests are physically and mentally demanding on the patient; thus, careful consideration must be given when deciding on and performing the indicated tests. These examinations are described as tools for diagnosing the causes and pathophysiology of FI, although some are performed in patients with constipation. A. Physiological examination Among the anorectal physiology examinations, five are covered by national health insurance: anorectal manometry, rectoanal inhibitory reflex test, rectal sensation test, rectal compliance test, and simulated defecation test. The medical fee is 800 points for one of these five tests and 1,200 points for two or more tests, which can be reimbursed only once a month. Among these, simulated defecation tests, such as the rectal balloon expulsion test, are used to diagnose functional defecation disorder, which is a type of constipation. Therefore, in this section, in addition to anorectal manometry, rectoanal inhibitory reflex test, and rectal sensation test, the PNTML and anal electromyography are described. 1. Anorectal manometry Statement • Anorectal manometry is proposed to be performed on a case-by-case basis because it can be useful for identifying the causes of fecal incontinence and guiding specialized treatment plans by objectively assessing anal sphincter function. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract The primary measurement parameters include the functional anal canal length, resting anal pressure, and voluntary contraction pressure (measured value and incremental value). Resting anal pressure is considered to reflect the internal anal sphincter (IAS) function; however, some reports indicate that 55% of it is contributed by the IAS, 30% by the external anal sphincter (EAS), and 15% by the anal cushion. Voluntary contraction pressure reflects the EAS function; however, there are two types of voluntary contraction pressures, that is, the measured value from the atmospheric pressure and the incremental value from the resting anal pressure. The incremental value of the voluntary contraction pressure reflects the EAS function. Low resting anal pressure indicates poor IAS function, which predisposes patients to passive fecal incontinence (FI), whereas low voluntary contraction pressure indicates poor EAS function, which predisposes patients to urge FI. Anorectal manometry can help identify the causes of FI by objectively assessing the function of the anal sphincter. However, the reference values for resting anal pressure and voluntary contraction pressure vary greatly depending on individuals and sex as well as on measurement devices and methods; thus, care must be taken when interpreting the measured values. Commentary Three measurement devices are used for this test: water perfusion system, pressure transducer catheter, and microballoon catheter. Commentary Three measurement devices are used for this test: water perfusion system, pressure transducer catheter, and microballoon catheter. In the test using a catheter with a pressure measurement point only at the same level along the longitudinal axis of the catheter, it is necessary to withdraw the catheter to measure the pressure over the entire length of the anal canal. In contrast, the test using a catheter with multiple pressure measurement points at the same intervals along the longitudinal axis of the catheter can measure the anal canal pressure of the entire length of the anal canal while the catheter is stationary. This test is referred to as high-resolution anorectal manometry (HRAM)[ ]. The primary measurement parameters include the length of the anal canal reflecting the anal canal pressure (functional anal canal length), anal canal pressure at rest (resting anal pressure), anal canal pressure during anal sphincter contraction (voluntary contraction pressure), and anal canal pressure during coughing (involuntary contraction pressure)[ - ]. In addition, when the anal canal pressure is measured while the rectal balloon is inflated with approximately 50 mL of air, the pressure rises sharply, then falls below the resting anal pressure, and gradually recovers to near the resting anal pressure. The increased pressure phenomenon is called the rectoanal excitatory reflex (RAER), whereas the decrease and recovery phenomenon are called the rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR). Resting anal pressure is generally considered to reflect the IAS function; however, some reports indicate that 55% of it is contributed by the IAS, 30% by the EAS, and 15% by the anal cushion[ ]. Voluntary contraction pressure is generally considered to reflect the EAS function; however, there are two types of voluntary contraction pressures, namely the measured value from the atmospheric pressure and the incremental value from the resting anal pressure. The incremental value of the voluntary contraction pressure reflects the EAS function[ , ]. Involuntary contraction pressure reflects the reflex contraction of the EAS in response to an increase in intra-abdominal pressure caused by coughing[ ]. The RAER is a phenomenon in which the EAS contracts reflexively in response to the expansion of the rectal wall. When the sacral and/or pudendal nerves are impaired, the involuntary contraction pressure decreases and the RAER disappears[ ]. RAIR is a phenomenon in which the IAS relaxes in response to the expansion of the rectal wall and is an intramural reflex that occurs in the rectum and anus. The loss of this reflex indicates the possibility of Hirschsprung's disease, but is not directly relevant to the management of FI. According to a meta-analysis (13 papers, 2,981 patients)[ ] in which anal manometry was performed on patients with FI, low resting anal pressure was found in 44% of women and 27% of men, whereas low contraction pressure was found in 69% of women and 36% of men. Low resting anal pressure indicates poor IAS function, which predisposes to passive FI[ ], whereas low voluntary contraction pressure indicates poor EAS function, which predisposes to urge FI[ , ]. In a prospective study[ ] that investigated the influence of anorectal physiology tests on decision-making for the treatment of FI, 45 out of 90 patients with FI were planned for conservative therapy, whereas the remaining 45 were planned for surgical treatment in the pre-examination meeting by an expert team. However, after review based on the results of anal manometry, PNTML, and endoanal ultrasonography, 5 (11%) of the 45 patients scheduled for conservative therapy were changed to surgical treatment, whereas 4 (9%) of the 45 patients scheduled for surgical treatment were changed to conservative therapy. Although endoanal ultrasonography results were more influential, it was demonstrated that anorectal manometry also influenced the decision-making for the treatment of FI, as the examination results were assessed comprehensively. However, because the reference values for resting anal pressure and voluntary contraction pressure vary greatly depending on individuals and sex[ ] as well as on measurement devices and methods[ ], care must be taken when interpreting the measured values. Anorectal sensation tests The rectal balloon sensation test, which assesses the sensation of pressure on the rectal wall by balloon distension, and the anal mucosal electrosensitivity test, which assesses the sensation of electrical stimulation on the anal mucosa, are performed as objective assessments of anorectal sensation. a. Rectal balloon sensation test Statement • Rectal balloon sensation test is proposed to be performed on a case-by-case basis because it can be useful for identifying the causes of fecal incontinence and guiding specialized treatment plans by objectively assessing rectal hypersensitivity and hyposensitivity. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract In patients with irritable bowel syndrome or other disorders associated with urge fecal incontinence (FI) due to rectal hypersensitivity, diagnosis using the rectal balloon sensation test can help determine indications for normalization training of the rectal sensation, which is part of biofeedback therapy. Conversely, in patients with overflow passive FI associated with fecal impaction due to rectal hyposensitivity, diagnosis using the rectal balloon sensation test can help determine indications for bowel habit training or normalization training of the rectal sensation. However, the results of the rectal balloon sensation test should be interpreted with caution because they are influenced by not only rectal sensation but also rectal capacity and compliance. Although the anal mucosal electrosensitivity test is occasionally used in research, it is rarely employed in daily clinical practice. Commentary a. Rectal balloon sensation test This test assesses the sensation of pressure on the rectal wall by gradually inflating a balloon inserted into the rectum with air to measure the following three values[ , , , ]: • First sensation volume (FSV): The minimum volume at which the subject first feels a change in the inflated balloon, also referred to as the rectal threshold volume. • Urge volume (UV): The minimum volume that induces an urge to use the toilet for defecation. • Maximum tolerable volume (MTV): The maximum volume the subject can tolerate. The London classification by the International Anorectal Physiology Working Group (IAPWG)[ ] recommends diagnosing patients with rectal hypersensitivity if one or more of the three measurement items of FSV, UV, and MTV are below the reference value, while it recommends diagnosing patients with rectal hyposensitivity if two or more items are above the reference value. According to a meta-analysis of studies involving patients with FI (13 studies, 2,981 cases)[ ], rectal hypersensitivity was observed in 10% of women and 4% of men, whereas rectal hyposensitivity was noted in 7% of women and 19% of men. Rectal hypersensitivity can cause fecal urgency, urge FI, and frequent bowel movements[ ] and is often observed in patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS[ , ] in addition to radiation proctitis and ulcerative colitis. Thus, this test is useful for evaluating rectal sensitivity in these conditions[ , ]. According to Chan et al.[ ], 44% of patients with FI had rectal hypersensitivity, and these patients defecated significantly more frequently and had significantly more restricted daily activities than those with normal rectal sensitivity. In addition, rectal hypersensitivity is frequently observed in patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS[ ] and is correlated with its symptomatic severity[ ]. Furthermore, this test is also useful for evaluating the capacity of the neorectum after rectal resection[ ], as its results reflect not only rectal sensation but also rectal capacity and compliance. Improvement of FI symptoms by biofeedback therapy[ ] or drug therapy[ ] is reported to be correlated with improvement in rectal hypersensitivity. In contrast, the test results may not change significantly even if the FI symptoms improve; thus, interpretation of the test results may be difficult in some cases[ ]. Rectal hyposensitivity can cause constipation[ ] and/or overflow passive FI[ , , ] associated with rectal fecal impaction due to difficulty in feeling the urge to defecate. This condition is often observed in patients with spinal cord impairment or older adults. Burgell et al.[ ] found that 26 (16%) of 160 male patients with FI had rectal hyposensitivity, and the prevalence of constipation symptoms was significantly higher in the rectal hyposensitivity

This condition is often observed in patients with spinal cord impairment or older adults. Burgell et al.[ ] found that 26 (16%) of 160 male patients with FI had rectal hyposensitivity, and the prevalence of constipation symptoms was significantly higher in the rectal hyposensitivity group than in the normal rectal sensitivity group. When rectal fecal impaction due to weakening or loss of the urge to defecate, associated with rectal hyposensitivity, is diagnosed as the cause of overflow passive FI, the FI symptoms may be improved by bowel habit training and normalization training of the rectal sensation using a rectal balloon[ ]. As described above, evaluation of abnormal rectal sensitivity by this test can elucidate the pathophysiology and causes of FI[ ], which may be useful for guiding treatment plans, and may improve FI symptoms through normalization of rectal sensitivity[ , , ]. However, care must be taken when interpreting the test results because they are influenced not only by rectal sensation but also by rectal capacity and compliance. In addition, reference values should be established for each facility because the test results differ depending on the shape and compliance of the balloon used and the test method, including the balloon inflation speed[ ]. Furthermore, although extremely rare, there have been reports of rectal perforation in patients who underwent this test after rectal resection surgery[ ]; thus, extra caution is required in determining the indications and performing this test in patients who underwent rectal resection surgery. b. Anal mucosal electrosensitivity test This test assesses the anal mucosal electrosensitivity threshold at which the patient complains of stimulation sensation by gradually increasing the intensity of electrical stimulation to the anal mucosa after a catheter attached to the stimulation electrode is inserted into the anal canal. A diagnosis of anal hyposensitivity is made when the threshold value is greater than the upper limit of the reference value[ ], although reference values differ depending on the stimulator. This test is occasionally used in research but is rarely employed in daily clinical practice. 3. Pudendal nerve terminal motor latency Abstract This test is used to evaluate the presence or absence of pudendal neuropathy. Patients with fecal incontinence (FI) may have prolonged PNTML compared with those without FI (control group). This test is of little use for the management of FI because its results depend on the examiner's technique, and it has low reliability for evaluating pudendal neuropathy. Commentary In the PNTML test, an electrical stimulation electrode attached to the tip of the index finger of a glove is inserted into the rectum to electrically stimulate the pudendal nerve through the rectal wall near the ischial tuberosity. The contraction of the external anal sphincter caused by stimulation is detected by a receiving electrode attached to the base of the index finger in the anal canal ( )[ ]. The time from the electrical stimulation of the pudendal nerve to the contraction of the external anal sphincter is the PNTML, which is measured separately for the left and right sides to evaluate the presence or absence of pudendal neuropathy. In other words, when the PNTML is prolonged, a diagnosis of pudendal neuropathy is made[ ]. St. Mark's electrode is often used as the electrode for this test, and although the cutoff value of the conduction time varies slightly by institution, a diagnosis of pudendal neuropathy is often made when the PNTML is ≥2.2 ms[ , ] or 2.4 ms[ , ]. Although this test has been used historically for the management of FI[ , ], it is of low reliability as a test to evaluate pudendal neuropathy because its results are dependent on the examiner's technique and because it reflects only damage to nerve fibers with the fastest conduction velocity and cannot evaluate damage to nerve fibers with slower conduction velocity[ ]. Therefore, its usefulness and strength of recommendation for managing FI is currently considered to be low[ , ]. The ASCRS Clinical Practice Guidelines[ ] strongly recommend that this test should not be performed as a standard examination with a low level of evidence. 4. Three types of electrodes are used for the test: needle electrodes inserted into the anal sphincters, surface electrodes applied around the anus, and anal electrodes inserted into the anal canal. Anal electromyography Abstract This test evaluates the contractility and relaxation state of the external anal sphincter and the puborectalis muscle by measuring their electrical activities. Three types of electrodes are used for the test: needle electrodes inserted into the anal sphincters, surface electrodes applied around the anus, and anal electrodes inserted into the anal canal. Anal electromyography using the surface electrode or anal electrode has been used to diagnose the causes of fecal incontinence (FI); however, currently, it is often used as a therapeutic device to provide feedback to patients on the degree of anal sphincter contraction in biofeedback therapy for FI. Needle electrodes are mainly used in research due to the pain associated with needle insertion. Commentary This test evaluates the contraction and relaxation states of the external anal sphincter and the puborectal muscle by measuring their electrical activities. Three types of electrodes are used for the test: needle electrodes inserted into the anal sphincters, surface electrodes applied around the anus, and anal electrodes inserted into the anal canal[ , ]. With the needle electrode, the patient undergoes examination in the lateral position, and the site and degree of disruption of the anal sphincters can be diagnosed by evaluating the motor unit potential (MUP: electrical activity with a certain voltage and width), which is the electrical activity level of the anal sphincters, at each site[ ]. However, this approach is currently superseded by endoanal ultrasonography for the diagnosis of the site and degree of disruption[ ]. Because of the pain associated with needle electrode insertion, anal electromyography using a needle electrode is rarely performed in daily clinical practice and is mainly used for research[ ]. With the surface electrode and anal electrode, the patient can undergo examination either in the lateral or sitting position; however, in general, they only allow the evaluation of the contraction and relaxation states of the entire anal sphincter and cannot be used to evaluate the electrical activity level of the anal sphincters at each site. Recently, however, high-resolution anal electrodes with many electrodes have been developed[ ]. Although they allow the evaluation of the contraction and relaxation states of the anal sphincters at each site without insertion of the needle electrode, they are still in the research stage. Although anal electromyography has been used to diagnose the causes of FI[ , ], it is now often used as a therapeutic device to provide feedback to patients on the degree of anal sphincter contraction in biofeedback therapy for FI[ , ]. In addition, it is used to diagnose pelvic floor incoordination, in which the external anal sphincter and puborectal muscle, which should normally remain relaxed, contract during straining for defecation[ ]. Moreover, it is used in biofeedback therapy for functional defecation disorder caused by pelvic floor incoordination, which is one of the causes of constipation[ , ]. B. Morphological examination 1. Ultrasonography Statement • Because endoanal ultrasonography is useful for diagnosing anal sphincter injury, it is proposed to be used for identifying the causes of fecal incontinence. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B • Although endovaginal ultrasonography and transperineal ultrasonography can visualize puborectalis muscle injury and pelvic organs, their diagnostic accuracy for anal sphincter injury is lower than that of endoanal ultrasonography. Thus, they are proposed to be used in situations where endoanal ultrasonography is not available. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Endoanal ultrasonography is a minimally invasive and simple examination method that requires the use of a dedicated probe, and it is useful for diagnosing internal and external anal sphincter injuries, tears, scarring, and atrophy, as well as for measuring the thickness of the anal sphincters. It has been reported that the incidence of fecal incontinence (FI) in obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS) increases with the severity of the anal sphincter injury diagnosed by ultrasonography. In addition, it has also been reported that OASIS was diagnosed in 30% of women with anal incontinence who underwent endoanal ultrasonography, although not clinically diagnosed with OASIS at the time of vaginal delivery. Therefore, endoanal ultrasonography is the most useful examination method for diagnosing OASIS. Thus, we propose using it for diagnosing the pathophysiology and causes of FI. Endovaginal ultrasonography can be performed with a probe used in obstetrics and gynecology and is superior to endoanal ultrasonography in the visualization of puborectalis muscle injury and pelvic floor opening formed by the levator ani, called the levator hiatus, which are difficult to diagnose by endoanal ultrasonography. However, its diagnostic accuracy for OASIS is lower than that of endoanal ultrasonography. Transperineal ultrasonography can be

not clinically diagnosed with OASIS at the time of vaginal delivery. Therefore, endoanal ultrasonography is the most useful examination method for diagnosing OASIS. Thus, we propose using it for diagnosing the pathophysiology and causes of FI. Endovaginal ultrasonography can be performed with a probe used in obstetrics and gynecology and is superior to endoanal ultrasonography in the visualization of puborectalis muscle injury and pelvic floor opening formed by the levator ani, called the levator hiatus, which are difficult to diagnose by endoanal ultrasonography. However, its diagnostic accuracy for OASIS is lower than that of endoanal ultrasonography. Transperineal ultrasonography can be performed using a versatile convex-type probe, and it allows for the visualization of the anal canal and a wide range of pelvic organs. In addition, it can evaluate still images, evaluate pelvic floor muscle contraction, and diagnose pelvic floor organ prolapse during straining. The use of a dedicated probe capable of 3D/4D construction allows for the diagnosis of injuries to the anal sphincters and puborectalis muscle, and it has been reported that its diagnostic accuracy for OASIS is comparable to that of endoanal ultrasonography. Based on the above, endoanal ultrasonography is most recommended for the diagnosis of anal sphincter injuries, including OASIS. However, in facilities where such test equipment is not available, we propose diagnosing them with endovaginal or transperineal ultrasonography, although their diagnostic accuracy is lower. Commentary a. Endoanal ultrasonography In endoanal ultrasonography, a dedicated radial or linear probe is inserted into the anus to visualize and evaluate the morphology of the internal and external anal sphincters by ultrasound. The patient is positioned in the prone or lithotomy position during examination to avoid left-right differences, but the test is often performed in the supine position to avoid embarrassment. In the ultrasound images, the internal anal sphincter is visualized as a uniformly concentric hypoechoic area, whereas the external anal sphincter is visualized as a medium- to hyperechoic area on the outside[ ], and different structures are visualized depending on the height of the anal canal ( ). Starting from the cranial side, at the upper level, the concentric deep external anal sphincter and the U-shaped puborectalis muscle are visualized as a hyperechoic area on the outside of the internal anal sphincter. At the middle level, the subcutaneous and superficial external anal sphincter, including the combined longitudinal muscle, is visualized as a medium-echoic area on the outside of the hypoechoic internal anal sphincter. At the lower level, only the subcutaneous external anal sphincter is visualized as a hyperechoic ring, whereas the internal anal sphincter is not visualized at this level. These differences in echo images that vary depending on the height of the anal canal are important for lesion orientation. This test is used to diagnose anal sphincter injury, laceration (a condition in which the anal sphincters remain cut with no signs of repair), scarring, atrophy, and to evaluate the morphology of the anal sphincters by measuring the thickness of the anal sphincters. Injuries to the external anal sphincter can be diagnosed by the depiction of hypoechoic areas in the hyperechoic area, whereas injuries to the internal anal sphincter can be diagnosed by the depiction of hyperechoic areas in the hypoechoic area. Once the examiner is skilled in the test, there should be no significant difference in diagnosis between examiners, making this test highly accurate[ ]. It has been reported that the prevalence of severe FI was 20 times higher in patients diagnosed with external anal sphincter injury by this test than in patients diagnosed as not having such injury[ ]. In particular, this test is considered the most useful test for diagnosing OASIS[ , ]. The guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists[ ] recommends classifying third-degree perineal lacerations (lacerations with injury extending to the anal sphincters) into 3a (injury that is less than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter), 3b (injury extending to more than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter but not extending to the internal anal sphincter), and 3c (injury to both internal and external anal sphincters). Based on their experience with 1,892 OASIS cases, Wan et al.[ ] reported that, compared with patients with OASIS grade 3a, patients with OASIS grade 3b or above had a higher incidence of FI, lower anal pressure, persistent anal sphincter defects in endoanal ultrasonography, a higher incidence of fistula formation, and a higher need for anal sphincter re-suturing. In addition, Johannessen et al.[ ] found that patients with OASIS grade 3c and 4 were at a higher risk of developing FI than patients with OASIS grade 3b and below ( : OASIS). Wan et al.[ ] performed this test on 134 patients with anal incontinence despite no clinical diagnosis of OASIS after childbirth and found OASIS in 40 patients (30%). A

patients with OASIS grade 3b or above had a higher incidence of FI, lower anal pressure, persistent anal sphincter defects in endoanal ultrasonography, a higher incidence of fistula formation, and a higher need for anal sphincter re-suturing. In addition, Johannessen et al.[ ] found that patients with OASIS grade 3c and 4 were at a higher risk of developing FI than patients with OASIS grade 3b and below ( : OASIS). Wan et al.[ ] performed this test on 134 patients with anal incontinence despite no clinical diagnosis of OASIS after childbirth and found OASIS in 40 patients (30%). A meta-analysis of studies evaluating the relationship between anal incontinence and the diagnosis of OASIS by ultrasonography (103 papers, 16,110 cases)[ ] showed that 26% of women post vaginal delivery were diagnosed with OASIS by ultrasonography, and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 19%. In addition, among 3,688 patients not clinically suspected of OASIS, 13% were diagnosed with OASIS by ultrasonography, and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 14%. Furthermore, of 7,549 patients who had undergone anal sphincter repair for OASIS, 55% had residual anal sphincter defects on ultrasonography, and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 38%. Compared with patients without OASIS on ultrasonography, the prevalence of anal incontinence was significantly higher (3.74 times) in patients diagnosed with OASIS. Therefore, the meta-analysis has demonstrated the importance of using ultrasonography to diagnose the presence or absence of OASIS in patients not clinically diagnosed with OASIS. In addition, this test is useful for evaluating the degree of repair after anal sphincter repair or sphincteroplasty for OASIS[ ]. Furthermore, even if FI does not develop immediately after vaginal delivery, it may develop due to OASIS after the age of 40 years, and this test is useful for diagnosing this condition[ , ]. This test is also useful for diagnosing internal anal sphincter injury and atrophy. Passive FI associated with internal anal sphincter injury may occur after lateral internal anal sphincterotomy for anal fissures, after radical anal Fistula treatment, or in rare cases, after ligation and resection of internal hemorrhoids, and this test is useful for diagnosing these conditions[ ]. In addition, the internal anal sphincter thickens with age, and the 95% confidence interval of the thickness of the internal anal sphincter in healthy individuals has been reported to be 2.4-2.7 mm for those under 55 years of age and 2.8-3.4 mm for those over 55 years of age[ ]. Internal anal sphincter degeneration has been reported as a condition in which the internal anal sphincter atrophies[ ]. It is characterized by passive FI as the main complaint, with low maximum resting pressure (<40 cmH 2 O) and thinning of the internal anal sphincter (<2 mm in thickness), and this test is useful for diagnosing this condition. b. Endovaginal ultrasonography Endovaginal ultrasonography uses either a linear or radial probe, as in endoanal ultrasonography, but probes commonly used in obstetrics and gynecology can be used. In the lithotomy position, a probe is inserted into the vagina, and 3D images are constructed to evaluate the pelvic floor structure. The images are divided into four sections based on the height in the axial plain, and starting from the cranial side, the bladder area and rectum can be visualized and evaluated at level I, the bladder neck, urethra and anorectal angle at level II, the urethra and puborectalis muscle at level III, and the perineal muscles, such as the superficial transverse perineal muscles, and the middle-lower anal canal at level IV[ ] ( ). Endovaginal ultrasonography is excellent for visualizing the puborectalis muscle and levator hiatus. Puborectalis muscle injury is observed in 13%-36% of primiparas who have had a vaginal delivery[ ]. However, it is difficult to diagnose puborectalis muscle injury by endoanal ultrasonography. In addition, injury to the pubovisceral muscle (a muscle group combining the puborectalis and pubococcygeus muscles) and dilation of the levator hiatus, diagnosed by endovaginal ultrasonography, are associated with the severity of FI[ ]. Therefore, although endovaginal ultrasonography is useful for visualizing the puborectalis muscle and levator hiatus, it is inferior to endoanal ultrasonography in the visualization of the anal sphincters themselves and the diagnosis of anal sphincter injury, which are the most important factors in the diagnosis of OASIS[ ]. c.
