Transperineal ultrasonography Transperineal ultrasonography uses a versatile convex-type probe, which is also used in abdominal ultrasonography, to scan the perineum from the pubic bone to the anus in the lithotomy position to visualize and evaluate pelvic organs (bladder, urethra, vaginal wall, anal canal, and rectum) and pelvic floor muscles, such as the puborectalis muscles, in the midsagittal section[ ] ( ). It allows the evaluation of static images as well as the evaluation of pelvic floor muscle contraction and the observation of pelvic floor organ prolapse (cystocele, uterine prolapse, rectocele, and enterocele) during the Valsalva maneuver. Its diagnostic accuracy for rectocele, enterocele, rectal intussusception, and rectal prolapse was superior to that of defecography[ ]. The use of a dedicated probe capable of 3D construction or 4D construction, including the time axis, allows for the diagnosis of injuries to the anal sphincters and puborectalis muscle through the construction of axial tomographic images. In the visualization of the anal sphincters themselves and in the diagnosis of anal sphincter injury, which are the most important factors for diagnosing OASIS, transperineal ultrasonography has been reported to be inferior to endoanal ultrasonography[ ], whereas another report has stated that transperineal ultrasonography using a 3D/4D probe is not inferior to endoanal ultrasonography[ ]. Therefore, the choice of whether to perform endoanal or transperineal ultrasonography for diagnosing OASIS depends on the skill and preference of the examiner and the availability of the examination equipment. Although endoanal ultrasonography requires a dedicated probe, it is relatively easy to master because it provides easy anatomic orientation. In contrast, while transperineal ultrasonography itself can be performed with a versatile abdominal ultrasound probe, it can achieve the same diagnostic accuracy for OASIS as endoanal ultrasonography if a dedicated 3D/4D probe is used, but it is relatively difficult to master, as anatomic orientation is difficult. 2. Pelvic MRI Statement • Anal MRI is proposed to be performed for identifying the causes of fecal incontinence because it is useful for evaluating the presence or absence and the degree of disruption or atrophy of the anal sphincters and pelvic floor muscles. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Pelvic MRI performed for the management of fecal incontinence (FI) includes anal MRI and MRI defecography. There are two types of anal MRI, namely endoanal MRI, which is performed by placing a dedicated endoanal coil in the anal canal, and external phased-array MRI, which is performed by placing a coil on the body surface. However, in Japan, only external phased-array MRI can be performed because the endoanal coil is yet to be approved. Anal MRI can evaluate the presence or absence of disruption or atrophy of the anal sphincters and pelvic floor muscles by imaging the structure of these muscles. MRI defecography has an advantage over conventional fluoroscopic defecography in that it allows the evaluation of the condition of other pelvic organs, such as the uterus and bladder, while avoiding radiation exposure. However, it has a disadvantage in that it is more nonphysiological because the patient is required to expel artificial stool in the supine position. Because of the nonphysiological posture for artificial stool expulsion, sufficient straining cannot be achieved. Thus, the diagnostic accuracy of this test is lower than that of fluoroscopic defecography in diagnosing rectal intussusception or rectocele, which may cause FI. Commentary Pelvic MRI is a diagnostic imaging technique that uses nuclear magnetic resonance to assess pelvic organs, pelvic floor muscles, and anal sphincters. MRI used for the management of FI includes an anal MRI, which evaluates with static images, and MRI defecography, which evaluates the dynamic state[ ]. An international consensus has been reached on the terminology related to MRI and the interpretation of MRI images in the evaluation of pelvic floor dysfunction, including FI[ , ]. There are two types of anal MRI, namely endoanal MRI, which is performed by placing a dedicated endoanal coil in the anal canal, and external phased-array MRI, which is performed by placing a coil on the body surface. In Japan, however, only external phased-array MRI can be performed because the endoanal coil is yet to be approved. In general, endoanal MRI is considered to have higher resolution and diagnostic accuracy than external phased-array MRI, although a study reported that there was no difference between the two[ ]. Anal MRI can evaluate the presence or absence of disruption or atrophy of the anal sphincters and pelvic floor muscles by imaging the structure of these muscles[ ]. On T2-weighted images, ligaments and fascia are visualized as low signals, the EAS is visualized as relatively low signals, and fat and the internal anal sphincter (IAS) are visualized as high signals. In general, endoanal ultrasonography is more useful for the diagnosis of disruption or atrophy of the IAS

Anal MRI can evaluate the presence or absence of disruption or atrophy of the anal sphincters and pelvic floor muscles by imaging the structure of these muscles[ ]. On T2-weighted images, ligaments and fascia are visualized as low signals, the EAS is visualized as relatively low signals, and fat and the internal anal sphincter (IAS) are visualized as high signals. In general, endoanal ultrasonography is more useful for the diagnosis of disruption or atrophy of the IAS than for the diagnosis of the EAS, whereas endoanal MRI is considered more useful for the diagnosis of disruption or atrophy of the EAS than for the diagnosis of the IAS[ ]. However, it has been reported that there is no difference between the two in the diagnostic accuracy of anal sphincter disruption, with their sensitivity and positive predictive value for anal sphincter disruption diagnosed by intraoperative findings being 90% and 85% by endoanal ultrasonography and 81% and 89% by endoanal MRI, respectively[ ]. MRI defecography is an examination in which videos are recorded while the artificial stool injected into the rectum is expelled. In the management of FI, it is performed to diagnose rectal intussusception and rectocele, which are considered possible causes of FI[ , ]. This test has an advantage over conventional fluoroscopic defecography in that it allows the evaluation of the condition of other pelvic organs, such as the uterus and bladder, while avoiding radiation exposure. The disadvantage of this approach is that the patient is required to expel artificial stool in the supine position, making it more nonphysiological than fluoroscopic defecography, which is performed in the sitting position. Although MRI defecography that can be performed in the sitting position is also available, it is not widely used because it requires special MRI equipment[ ]. In addition, according to a meta-analysis, the diagnostic accuracy of MRI defecography for rectal intussusception or rectocele is lower than that of fluoroscopic defecography, as sufficient straining cannot be achieved because of the nonphysiological posture for artificial stool expulsion[ ]. Therefore, this test is considered less useful for diagnosing the causes of FI than fluoroscopic defecography. 3. Defecography Statement • Defecography is useful for diagnosing rectal intussusception and rectocele, which can cause fecal incontinence. Thus, it is proposed to be performed on a case-by-case basis. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Defecography (evacuation proctography) allows the evaluation of the anorectal angle, perineal descent, anal sphincter contractility, ability to expel artificial stool, and dynamics of the pelvic floor muscles and rectum during artificial stool expulsion. In addition, it allows the diagnosis of the presence or absence as well as the degree of rectocele, rectal intussusception, sigmoidocele, and enterocele. However, caution is required when interpreting the results, as these conditions can also be observed in healthy individuals without defecation disorders. Obtuse anorectal angle and excessive perineal descent are believed to be involved in the weakening of pelvic floor muscles, which may cause fecal incontinence (FI). However, it is impossible to evaluate the presence or absence as well as the degree of FI by these factors alone, as there are large individual differences even among healthy individuals. In addition, this test also allows the evaluation of anal sphincter contractility by assessing the ability to hold artificial stool in the rectum during the injection of artificial stool into the rectum and in the sitting position after the injection. In patients with FI who do not achieve adequate improvement with maximal conservative therapies, FI can be improved by ventral rectopexy if severe rectal intussusception or rectocele is found by defecography. Therefore, it is recommended to perform defecography on such patients. Commentary Defecography is an examination to evaluate the morphology and dynamics of the rectum and pelvic floor muscle group during defecation. Although its examination methods vary from institution to institution, recently, the ASCRS, in collaboration with five other international societies, has published a consensus on examination method and image interpretation[ ]. The general examination method involves injecting a mixture of contrast agent and a material for maintaining viscosity (artificial stool) into the rectum, placing the patient in the sitting position, and taking still and video X-ray images from the side and the front at rest during anal sphincter contraction and defecation. In some cases, barium or gastrografin is administered 30-120 minutes before the examination to simultaneously contrast the small intestine, or barium is injected before the injection of artificial stool to contrast the sigmoid colon. This examination allows the evaluation of the anorectal angle, perineal descent, anal sphincter contractility, ability to expel artificial stool, and dynamics of the pelvic floor muscles and rectum during artificial stool expulsion[ ]. In addition, it

In some cases, barium or gastrografin is administered 30-120 minutes before the examination to simultaneously contrast the small intestine, or barium is injected before the injection of artificial stool to contrast the sigmoid colon. This examination allows the evaluation of the anorectal angle, perineal descent, anal sphincter contractility, ability to expel artificial stool, and dynamics of the pelvic floor muscles and rectum during artificial stool expulsion[ ]. In addition, it also allows the diagnosis of the presence or absence, as well as the degree of rectocele, rectal intussusception, sigmoidocele, and enterocele. However, caution is required when interpreting the results, as these conditions can also be observed in healthy individuals without defecation disorders[ , ]. Obtuse anorectal angle and excessive perineal descent are believed to be involved in the weakening of pelvic floor muscles, including the puborectalis muscle, which may cause FI[ ]. The anorectal angle is reported to be significantly more obtuse in patients with FI than in individuals without FI (a mean of 105° vs. 116° at rest)[ ]. However, it is impossible to evaluate the presence or absence as well as the degree of FI by these factors alone, as the anorectal angle and perineal descent vary substantially among individuals, even among healthy individuals. In addition, this test also allows the evaluation of anal sphincter contractility by assessing the ability to hold artificial stool in the rectum during the injection of artificial stool into the rectum and in the sitting position after the injection[ ]. Furthermore, by performing this test using artificial stool containing gastrografin to evaluate the ability to hold artificial stool before closing the temporary stoma created at the time of rectal resection, the state of fecal continence when the temporary stoma is closed can be predicted[ ]. This test is mainly used for diagnosing defecation disorder, which is a form of constipation. However, because the usefulness of ventral rectopexy (VR) for FI associated with rectal intussusception or rectocele was reported[ ], this test has also been used in the treatment of FI[ ]. The mechanism by which rectal intussusception causes FI is unclear, but possible mechanisms include induction of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex[ ] and a decrease in resting anal canal pressure[ ]. Collinson et al.[ ] proposed the Oxford classification (grades I to V) to categorize the severity of rectal intussusception using this test and reported that this test performed on 40 patients in whom the cause of FI could not be diagnosed by rectoanal function tests or endoanal ultrasonography revealed rectal intussusception in 63% of the patients. Hawkins et al.[ ] performed this test on 147 patients with FI and reported that the more severe the rectal intussusception, the more severe the FI. In addition, Tsunoda et al.[ ] also reported that the degree of descent of the anterior wall in rectal intussusception was significantly correlated with the severity of FI. Furthermore, a systematic review of the outcomes of VR for rectal intussusception (10 studies, 1,147 patients)[ ] found that FI improved in 62.5% of patients, and the symptom recurrence rate was 7.3%. In other words, in patients with FI who do not achieve adequate improvement with maximal conservative therapies, FI may be improved by VR if severe rectal intussusception (grade III [presenting part reaching the upper edge of the anal canal] and grade IV [presenting part inside the anal canal] according to the Oxford classification) is found by defecography. Therefore, it is recommended to perform defecography on such patients. The mechanism by which rectocele causes FI is also unclear, but a possible mechanism is that stool that is not completely expelled during defecation and remains in the rectocele leaks out after defecation[ ]. Formijne et al.[ ] performed VR on patients with rectocele and enterocele and reported that the percentage of patients with FI was significantly reduced from 63% to 18%. In contrast, Wong et al.[ ] performed VR on 84 patients with rectocele and reported significant improvement in vaginal discomfort and symptoms of defecation disorder but no improvement in FI. In addition, Tsunoda et al.[ ] performed transanal repair in 30 patients with rectocele and reported that FI improved in 3 of 5 patients (60%) with FI before surgery; however, 4 of 25 patients (16%) without FI before surgery developed FI. Therefore, in the treatment of FI, defecography appears to be less significant in the diagnosis of rectocele than in that of rectal intussusception. IV. Conservative Therapies for Fecal Incontinence Conservative therapies for fecal incontinence (FI) include dietary therapy, bowel habit instructions, drug therapy, pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), biofeedback therapy, and transanal irrigation. The main goals are to solidify stool consistency, increase the contractility of pelvic floor muscles including the external anal sphincter, normalize rectal sensation, and periodically empty the rectum and colon. Among these interventions, dietary therapy, bowel habit instructions, and drug therapy can be provided with some degree of knowledge and experience and should be actively performed as initial conservative therapies even at medical institutions that do not specialize in defecation disorders. In contrast, PFMT, biofeedback therapy, and transanal irrigation require patient education and instructions based on expert knowledge and experience. Thus, they are best performed as specialized conservative therapies at institutions that specialize in defecation disorders. The package insert of the nerve stimulation device used for sacral neuromodulation, which has been covered by insurance in Japan since 2014, explicitly states that this therapy is indicated for “patients who have failed or are not suitable for conservative therapies”. In addition, the calculation criteria for the home transanal self-irrigation instructions and management fee for transanal irrigation, which has been covered by insurance since 2018, specify that this therapy is indicated for “patients with defecation disorders caused by spinal cord injury (excluding patients after rectal surgery) who do not achieve adequate improvement even with conservative therapies for 3 months or longer”. Thus, conservative therapies should be attempted first for FI caused by benign conditions. For various conservative therapies to be appropriately selected and implemented in Japan, the characteristics of each therapy must be well understood. This section provides an overview and explanation of each therapy. A. Initial conservative therapy 1. Dietary therapy Statement • Dietary fiber intake is recommended in treating fecal incontinence associated with soft stools. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B • For fecal incontinence accompanied by loose stools, it is recommended to avoid alcohol consumption and foods that soften the stool. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 81.8%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Because fecal incontinence (FI) is more likely to occur with increased defecation frequency and softer stools, we aim to optimize stool consistency and defecation frequency by assessing food intake and indulgences that affect defecation as well as planning and instructing an appropriate dietary therapy appropriate for each patient. Commentary Although there is little evidence on the usefulness of dietary therapy for FI, some randomized controlled trials (RCTs) indicate that dietary fiber supplements, such as psyllium, alleviate FI by improving stool consistency[ , ]. An RCT found that dietary fiber intake, in addition to the intake of antidiarrheals, such as loperamide, improved FI[ ]. According to a prospective observational study that followed approximately 60,000 older women over a long period, the group with the highest dietary fiber intake (25 g/day) had a 31% lower risk of watery stools and an 18% lower risk of FI than those in the group with the lowest dietary fiber intake (13.5 g/day)[ ]. Foods rich in fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAPs) can cause diarrhea and the urge to defecate. Thus, a low-FODMAP diet is considered effective for improving FI with soft stools[ ]. In an RCT comparing the effects of a low-FODMAP diet and psyllium on FI, the frequency of FI was reduced by more than 50% in 38.9% and 50% of patients, respectively, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups[ ]. In contrast, in an RCT in which older stroke patients with reduced physical strength were instructed to modify their diet and fluid intake to regulate defecation, the frequency of defecation was optimized, but FI was not reduced[ ]. Patients are advised to avoid caffeine, citrus fruits, spicy foods, and foods high in fat, as these have the effect of softening the stool. Limiting alcohol intake may also be effective[ ]. A study reported that the symptoms of FI (evaluated by the FISI) and FI-specific QoL (evaluated by the FIQL) were significantly improved when patients with FI were instructed to consume more white rice than bread or noodles and to limit the consumption of fruits, sweets, milk, yogurt, fat, caffeinated drinks, and alcoholic drinks[ ]. Although white rice contains little dietary fiber, nondigestible starch (resistant starch), which is abundant in white rice, exhibits the same physiological activity as soluble and insoluble dietary fiber in the intestinal tract[ ]. Bowel habit instructions Statement • The acquisition of bowel habits through appropriate instructions is recommended to be included in the treatment of fecal incontinence. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Continued accumulation of feces in the rectum is likely to cause fecal incontinence (FI). Thus, patients should defecate promptly without holding back as soon as they feel the urge to defecate. In addition, in conditions where patients do not feel the urge to defecate because of spinal cord injury or other causes, they should empty the rectum periodically by bowel habit training, in which patients attempt to defecate regularly even when they do not feel the urge to defecate. Commentary Bowel habit instructions are an important component of FI treatment. Patients with normal rectal sensation should be encouraged to go to the toilet promptly without holding back as soon as they feel the urge to defecate. Meanwhile, in patients with rectal hyposensation, emptying the rectum through planned defecation involving planned attempts to defecate even when no urge to defecate is felt can significantly improve FI[ , ]. In older adults and patients with spinal cord injury, if feces continue to accumulate in the rectum and no urge to defecate is felt even if there is feces in the rectum, rectal fecal impaction may occur, resulting in overflow passive FI. These patients may benefit from bowel habit training, wherein they go to the toilet twice a day (30 minutes after breakfast and dinner) to defecate even if they do not feel the urge to defecate (abdominal pressure defecation). Nurse-led education and advice on bowel habits can alleviate FI[ ]. In contrast, in an RCT of 112 patients with FI admitted to a nursing home, dietary and exercise instructions, as well as bowel habit instructions including toilet assistance, significantly increased food and fluid intake, physical activity, and frequency of defecation but did not decrease the frequency of FI[ ]. In addition, Ouslander et al.[ ] applied a urinary incontinence treatment method called “promoted voiding” to patients with FI in a nursing home and found that the frequency of normal bowel movements increased significantly, although the frequency of FI did not decrease significantly. The authors suggest that encouraging patients to urinate and defecate, according to their own will, can prevent constipation and fecal impaction by increasing toilet mobility and fluid intake, and they highlight the need for comprehensive behavioral therapy specifically tailored to treat FI. 3. Care for fecal incontinence Statement • For prevention and treatment of fecal IAD, it is recommended to gently wipe or clean the skin with products other than soap (alkaline) and to keep it moisturized with a moisturizer. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: A Abstract Important care for patients with refractory fecal incontinence (FI) includes planned defecation through bowel habit instructions, the use of pads and diapers, and prevention and care for IAD. Because the care varies substantially among individuals depending on the state of FI and age, it is important to provide care based on a thorough assessment of the condition of each patient. Commentary Care must be provided to patients with refractory FI such that FI does not become a social or hygienic problem in daily life. In nursing homes, the most common care for older adults with FI is the use of pads and diapers (88.9%), followed by planned defecation (38.6%)[ ]. For the methods and usefulness of planned defecation through bowel habit instructions, please refer to “IV-A-2. Bowel Habit Instructions”. The use of appropriate absorbent products, such as pads and diapers, is essential for FI management. A survey of local residents regarding FI revealed that panty liners and sanitary pads, which can be changed frequently, were the most commonly used products, whereas pads and diapers designed for urinary incontinence were used by those with urinary incontinence in addition to watery stools and FI. The use of appropriate absorbent products, such as pads and diapers, is essential for FI management. A survey of local residents regarding FI revealed that panty liners and sanitary pads, which can be changed frequently, were the most commonly used products, whereas pads and diapers designed for urinary incontinence were used by those with urinary incontinence in addition to watery stools and FI. The ratings for comfort and effectiveness against FI varied by product and individual, but odor control was rated low for all products[ ]. The most cost-effective absorbent products for moderate to severe FI were disposable diapers for men and pads for women, indicating a gender difference. However, because of large individual differences, such as differences in preferences and lifestyles, it is not possible to determine the most useful type of product[ ]. Because IAD occurs when stool comes into prolonged contact with the skin, prompt removal of stool attached to the skin is a basic principle to prevent IAD[ ]. However, there are no studies with a high level of evidence on absorbent products for preventing IAD caused by FI[ ]. The most effective method to prevent IAD is to keep moisture sources and irritants resulting from incontinence away from the skin to avoid skin maceration and contact with irritants[ , ]. A skin care method that is less irritating to the skin is the use of wet wipes containing a cleansing agent, moisturizer, and skin protectant (hereafter referred to as “triple-agent wet wipes”)[ ]. According to an RCT[ ] comparing the incidence of IAD, the incidence was significantly lower with triple-agent wet wipes at 8.1% than with water and soap at 27.1%. These wet wipes are sold as “butt wipes” by various manufacturers in Japan. Alkaline soap is a chemical irritant to the skin. Thus, it should be avoided whenever possible[ ]. A Cochrane review has shown that standardized skin care using triple-agent wet wipes may be more effective than skin care with water and soap for the prevention and treatment of IAD[ ]. However, if wet wipes are not sufficient to remove stool attached to the skin, it is recommended to wash the skin using a skin cleaning agent or a mildly acidic (pH 5.5-7.0) skin cleanser and rinse off with lukewarm water[ ]. When washing and rinsing, care should be taken to minimize mechanical irritation to the skin by lathering and gently washing the skin without using sponges or towels[ ]. After cleansing, an emollient-based moisturizer, such as Vaseline, olive oil, and mineral oil, should be used[ ]. The purpose is to replenish the intercellular lipids (hydrolipid film) of the skin and maintain normal barrier function by slowing down moisture loss from the skin. Furthermore, an RCT has shown that, in severe cases of IAD, the use of water-repellent skin protectants reduces erythema, increases the moisture content of the stratum corneum, and shifts the skin pH toward a slightly acidic level[ ]. Moreover, a systematic review has shown that the use of IAD assessment tools, skin cleansers with a pH of 4.0-6.8, changing body position, and high-protein diet intake are effective prevention and care methods for IAD in older adults[ ]. When perianal skin erosions are present as a form of IAD, in addition to standard skin care involving skin wiping, cleansing, and moisturizing, a powdered (CMC-based) skin protectant, which is a stoma care product, should be sprinkled on the affected area, followed by the application of a skin film agent[ ]. If ulcers are present, consultation with a dermatologist or other healthcare professional should be considered to differentiate IAD from other diseases, such as Crohn's disease and herpes[ ]. 4. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract Currently, there is no prescription drug indicated for the treatment of fecal incontinence (FI) in Japan. However, many cases of FI are associated with defecation abnormalities, such as diarrhea and constipation. Thus, drugs that are indicated for these conditions can be used. In general, the looser the stool consistency and the more frequent the bowel movements, the greater the amount and frequency of incontinence. Therefore, in treating FI associated with soft or watery stools, antidiarrheals are used to solidify stool consistency and inhibit peristalsis of the large intestine. In contrast, suppositories and enemas are used to void the rectum in treating FI associated with defecation disorder and overflow FI. In treating FI associated with diarrhea caused by inappropriate or excessive use of laxatives, the type and dosage of laxatives should be adjusted appropriately. Commentary Major overseas guidelines recommend solidifying stool consistency using stool bulking agents, such as dietary fiber, and antidiarrheals as the initial treatment for FI[ , ]. Drugs that have been evaluated in RCTs for their efficacy in the treatment of FI include loperamide hydrochloride, psyllium (dietary fiber supplement), diphenoxylate (a natural opioid), codeine phosphate, tricyclic antidepressants, sucralfate, and methylcellulose[ , - ]. Of these, loperamide hydrochloride is the only drug that has been thoroughly investigated and confirmed to be effective[ , - ]. There are several other drugs effective in treating FI, although the level of evidence is not high. The appropriate drug should be selected based on the presence of defecation abnormalities (such as soft stools, watery stools, and incomplete defecation) associated with FI. a. Calcium polycarbophil Calcium polycarbophil (CP), used in Japan as a therapeutic drug for IBS, is a calcium salt of a high molecular weight absorbent polymer that becomes polycarbophil by releasing calcium ions under acidic conditions in the stomach, and it acts by absorbing intestinal liquid that is >35 times of its original weight under neutral conditions in the small and large intestines, swelling and gelling, and being almost 100% evacuated in the stool without being absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract. Because it softens hard stools and solidifies watery stools, it is used in both diarrhea-predominant and constipation-predominant IBS and is expected to be effective as a stool bulking agent in treating FI through the same mechanisms as dietary fiber[ ]. CP is the most commonly prescribed drug for FI at major specialized facilities in Japan[ ]. In contrast, CP is mainly sold as an over-the-counter drug overseas, and no RCT has been conducted on its use in patients with FI. In a 6-month RCT conducted overseas on patients with IBS, frequent bowel movements significantly improved in the CP 6 g/day group compared with that in the placebo group[ ]. In Japan, Shibata et al.[ ] conducted an RCT involving 21 patients after total colectomy and ileal pouch anal anastomosis and found that nocturnal soiling decreased in the CP group. In a case series by Abe et al.[ ], 72 patients with FI of various stool consistency were treated with CP (0.5-1 g three times a day), and the median CCFIS improved significantly from 11 to 5, with side effects such as constipation, hard stools, and abdominal distention observed in 14% of the patients. b. Loperamide hydrochloride Loperamide hydrochloride is a potent antidiarrheal that acts on opioid receptors of the small and large intestines to inhibit peristalsis, inhibit the secretion of water and electrolytes in the intestinal tract, and facilitate absorption, thereby reducing the frequency of defecation and solidifying stool consistency. It is useful for the treatment of patients suffering from FI associated with loose stools, but excessive administration may cause constipation symptoms; thus, the dosage must be titrated depending on individual patients. As a guideline, bowel movements should be adjusted to range from every other day to twice a day, with stool consistency between types 3 and 4 of the Bristol Stool Form Scale[ , , ]. If constipation symptoms occur even with 1-mg capsules, the dosage should be gradually increased starting with 0.5 mg/day using granules. Although 2 mg/day is the upper limit of the treatment dosage covered by insurance, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that the dosage can be increased up to 16 mg/day until the ideal stool consistency has been reached, as this drug is safe and effective in a dose-dependent manner[ ]. B. Specialized conservative therapy 1. Pelvic floor muscle training Statement • PFMT with proper instructions is proposed for the treatment of fecal incontinence. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Abstract PFMT is a treatment that improves urinary and fecal incontinence (FI) by increasing the contractility of pelvic floor muscles, such as the levator ani and external anal sphincter, through contraction training. Because the type of patients with FI benefiting from PFMT is not known, it is indicated for patients who can fully understand the instructions and are motivated to continue PFMT at home. The efficacy rate of properly instructed PFMT in treating FI has been reported to be 41%-66%. Commentary PFMT, also called Kegel exercise, is a method advocated by the American obstetrician and gynecologist Kegel in the 1950s[ ]. Typically, patients are instructed to contract their pelvic floor muscles for 10 seconds and then rest for 20 seconds while breathing normally with relaxed abdominal and buttock muscles. In a single set, this contraction is repeated 10-20 times, and patients are instructed to perform three to five sets of this exercise every day[ ]. For patients who have difficulty maintaining sustained contractions, PFMT should be performed for as few seconds or as many times as possible. Although PFMT is generally instructed only verbally or in writing with a brochure, the effectiveness of the training is enhanced when therapists place their hand on the patients' abdomen and instruct the patients not to contract their abdominal muscles during the contraction exercise while checking the state of anal contraction by digital rectal examination or visual inspection and feeding back this information to the patients[ ]. In patients with urge FI, it is particularly important to train the patients to relax their abdominal muscles and contract their pelvic floor muscles because the patients' whole body tends to tense up when holding back the urge to defecate, resulting in increased abdominal pressure that may induce FI. Although a report stated that FI was significantly improved in the group that received PFMT instructions from a physical therapist compared with that in the group that received only a brochure on PFMT[ ], another report indicated that there was no significant difference between the two groups[ ]. Most RCTs evaluating the efficacy of PFMT are studies in which PFMT was evaluated as a control against biofeedback (BF) therapy[ , , ]. The efficacy rate of PFMT for FI ranged from 41% to 66%, with another report stating that it is less effective than BF therapy[ ] and others showing no significant difference between the two groups[ , ]. In an RCT verifying the effects of early postpartum PFMT instructed by a physical therapist, there was no difference in the frequency of anal incontinence between the group that received PFMT instructions and the group that did not; however, there was a significant increase in anal sphincter contractility and endurance in the group that received PFMT instructions[ ]. Although PFMT may have a lower efficacy rate than BF therapy, PFMT alone improved FI in 41% of patients who had not shown improvement with other conservative therapies[ ]. Therefore, PFMT is recommended with “Grade of Recommendation B” in the Incontinence 6 th Edition[ ] but is “weakly recommended” in the European guideline with a low level of evidence[ ]. 2. Biofeedback therapy Statement • Biofeedback therapy is proposed to be performed for the treatment of fecal incontinence. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B Abstract Biofeedback therapy is a type of pelvic floor physiotherapy that employs engineering devices to effectively impart pelvic floor muscle training. Its purpose is to strengthen and sustain the contractility of the pelvic floor muscles, including the external anal sphincter, and to normalize rectal sensation through three methods, namely pelvic floor muscle contraction training, pelvic floor muscle coordination training, and normalization training of the rectal sensation. Because it is not known what type of patients with fecal incontinence (FI) will benefit from biofeedback therapy, this therapy is indicated for patients with normal vision and hearing to recognize indicators from engineering devices and who can fully understand the instructions. The efficacy rate of biofeedback therapy for FI has been reported to be 70%-80%, with an odds ratio of 1.2 (0.7-2.1) according to a meta-analysis of RCTs comparing it with other treatments. Commentary Biofeedback (BF) therapy is a treatment method that converts physiological phenomena in the body that are normally difficult to recognize into sensory signals that can be perceived using engineering devices, allowing the phenomena to be voluntarily controlled. PFMT and BF therapy for FI are collectively called pelvic floor physiotherapy, which is a type of physical therapy. The goals of BF therapy are to strengthen and sustain the contractility of the pelvic floor muscles, including the external anal sphincter, and to normalize rectal sensation[ ]. Because the type of patients with FI benefiting from it is not known, BF therapy is indicated for patients who fully understand the instructions and are sufficiently motivated to continue pelvic floor muscle contraction training at home[ ]. Although the efficacy of BF therapy for FI has not yet been confirmed, it is considered to be a treatment that may be performed when other conservative therapies are ineffective, as it has no side effects[ , ]. Methods: The following methods are used alone or in combination depending on individual pathological condition[ , , ]. 1) Pelvic floor muscle contraction training This is a training to effectively strengthen the pelvic floor muscles, as patients themselves recognize the contraction state of their anal sphincter using anal manometry or electromyogram. The device used and the duration of treatment vary among institutions, and there is no standardized method. Generally, it is performed in an outpatient setting, and patients are instructed to perform three types of contraction methods, comprising the strongest contraction, prolonged contraction, and quick contraction, while the contraction state of the anal sphincters is fed back to the patients via waveforms on the display or signal sounds[ ]. Although it is important to contract only the pelvic floor muscles, some patients tend to tense up their abdominal and thigh muscles. Therefore, it is more effective to attach surface electromyographs to the abdomen and thighs and provide feedback to patients on the state of activity of these muscles[ ]. This outpatient instruction session is given once or twice a month, for a total of about five sessions. Patients are instructed to perform three to five sets of each of the three types of contraction training at home on a daily basis, each set consisting of 10 repetitions. Effects begin to appear several months after the start of treatment. The maximum voluntary contraction pressure and contraction duration (with the target being 10 s) are indicators to determine the effectiveness of the treatment. 2) Pelvic floor muscle coordination training This is a training to improve the coordination between rectal sensation and contraction of pelvic floor muscles, including the anal sphincters. When stool accumulates in the rectum, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex is induced, causing the anal canal to relax and making FI more likely. This condition is reproduced with a rectal balloon, and the patients are trained to prevent FI by conscious contraction of their pelvic floor muscles. As the rectal balloon is inflated, the patients would feel the urge to defecate, and they are instructed to contract their pelvic floor muscles at the same time. The goal is to achieve the strongest contraction within one second after the balloon is inflated[ ]. 3) Normalization training of the rectal sensation In general,

stool accumulates in the rectum, the rectoanal inhibitory reflex is induced, causing the anal canal to relax and making FI more likely. This condition is reproduced with a rectal balloon, and the patients are trained to prevent FI by conscious contraction of their pelvic floor muscles. As the rectal balloon is inflated, the patients would feel the urge to defecate, and they are instructed to contract their pelvic floor muscles at the same time. The goal is to achieve the strongest contraction within one second after the balloon is inflated[ ]. 3) Normalization training of the rectal sensation In general, rectal hyposensitivity tends to result in passive FI, whereas rectal hypersensitivity tends to result in urge FI[ ]. In patients with rectal hyposensitivity (with the first sensation volume >100 mL) by rectal balloon sensation test, the balloon inflation volume is decreased by 10% from the first sensation volume in increments to train the patients to perceive smaller volumes[ ]. This allows the patients to be aware of when to go to the toilet in time. In contrast, in patients diagnosed with rectal hypersensitivity (with the maximum tolerated volume <150 mL), the balloon inflation volume is gradually increased to train the patients to increase their tolerated volume. This allows the patients to hold their bowel movements until they go to the toilet. Sensation training was reported to be more effective than contraction training in improving FI symptoms[ ]. Effectiveness: Many studies evaluating pelvic floor physiotherapy for FI have been reported, including approximately 30 RCTs[ , , , ]. In addition, nine systematic reviews and meta-analyses that comprehensively evaluated these studies have been reported[ , , , - ]. The efficacy rate of BF therapy for FI is 70%-80%[ , , , ]. An RCT has reported that BF therapy (with an efficacy rate of 76%) was significantly more effective than PFMT (with an efficacy rate of 41%)[ ]. In contrast, BF therapy was reported to be as effective as drug therapy and PFMT[ ]. Therefore, the effectiveness of BF therapy has not been conclusively determined. This is attributed to the lack of uniformity in the frequency, duration, and methods of BF therapy as well as the differences in the instructing ability of therapists[ ]. According to a meta-analysis involving six RCTs, the odds ratio for the efficacy of BF therapy compared with other treatments was 1.2 (0.7-2.1)[ ], and a 2012 Cochrane review also concluded that the efficacy of BF therapy for FI is not definitive[ ]. Therefore, pelvic floor physiotherapy was rated as “moderately recommended” with a low level of evidence in the 2022 European guideline[ ]. In contrast, BF therapy, while requiring some specialized devices, effectively aids the instructions of PFMT without any side effects. Thus, it is “strongly recommended” with a moderate level of evidence in the 2021 ACG Clinical Guidelines[ ] and recommended with “Grade of Recommendation A” in the Incontinence 6 th Edition[ ]. Regarding the effects of pelvic floor physiotherapy on different pathological conditions, effects before and after anal sphincteroplasty for FI caused by anal sphincter injury during childbirth, effects for perinatal FI, and effects for LARS have been evaluated in systematic reviews. It has been reported to have some effect, although not remarkable[ , , ]. The effects of BF therapy are significantly enhanced when combined with medium-frequency anal electrical stimulation, and self-BF therapy at home is as effective as BF therapy at the hospital. These are subjects for future research[ , - ]. 3. Transanal irrigation Statement • Transanal irrigation is recommended only for patients with severe fecal incontinence when it is worth the time and effort required for irrigation. Strength of Recommendation: Strong (Consensus Rate: 90.9%), Level of Evidence: B Abstract Transanal irrigation, or retrograde colonic irrigation, is a treatment in which the rectum and left colon are periodically emptied by transanal irrigation. This treatment is indicated for patients with severe constipation or fecal incontinence (FI). It is indicated in patients with spinal cord injury and in children with spina bifida, who often have both symptoms of constipation and FI. Overseas, it is also applied for patients with defecation disorders following low anterior resection. In Japan, it is covered by insurance for patients with defecation disorders caused by spinal cord injury that do not improve adequately with conservative treatment for more than 3 months (excluding patients who have had rectal surgery). Commentary Transanal irrigation (TAI) is a bowel management technique in which 300-1,000 mL of warm water is infused transanally into the rectum via a balloon catheter daily or every other day to evacuate stool from the rectum to the descending colon[ ]. In TAI, the infusion of irrigation fluid requires approximately 15 minutes, and the complete evacuation of the infused warm water takes approximately 45 minutes. It can only be continued

Commentary Transanal irrigation (TAI) is a bowel management technique in which 300-1,000 mL of warm water is infused transanally into the rectum via a balloon catheter daily or every other day to evacuate stool from the rectum to the descending colon[ ]. In TAI, the infusion of irrigation fluid requires approximately 15 minutes, and the complete evacuation of the infused warm water takes approximately 45 minutes. It can only be continued if the patient has severe constipation or FI for which the effort and time are worth it. However, if treatment can be continued without undue psychological and physical burden, severe FI can be alleviated, and QoL can be improved[ - ]. The level of evidence regarding the utility of TAI for intractable defecation disorders is relatively high, as there are two RCTs[ , ], eight reviews, and numerous observational studies on it. In an RCT comparing TAI with other conservative treatments in 87 patients with neurogenic bowel dysfunction, the CCFIS, St. Mark's Score, and neurogenic bowel disorder (NBD) Score significantly improved in the TAI group[ ]. Additionally, a cost-effectiveness analysis using data from the same RCT showed that TAI was more cost-effective than other conservative treatments[ ]. In an observational study of 348 patients with bowel defecation disorders associated with various etiologies, 145 patients (42%) continued to use TAI during a mean follow-up period of 21 months. The treatment success rates were higher in patients with neurogenic bowel dysfunction (63%) and anorectal dysfunction (51%) and lower in patients with postoperative anorectal dysfunctions (29%) and idiopathic constipation (34%)[ ]. In addition, out of a total of 110,000 irrigation procedures, two cases of bowel perforation (one in the rectum and one in the sigmoid colon) occurred. Despite its low incidence, caution should be exercised. In Japan, the Peristeen Ⓡ anal irrigation system (Coloplast Japan, Tokyo) was approved in 2016 as a dedicated device for TAI. In 2017, a prospective multicenter study was conducted using this system in patients with intractable defecation disorders[ ]. Among the 32 patients (median age 55.5 years, 19 men) who initiated TAI, 25 (78%) completed the 10-week TAI, and 23 (72%) wished to continue TAI after the study had ended. Patient satisfaction with bowel movements was also significantly improved. However, colonic perforation was noted in three patients (9.4%). While one patient was healed conservatively, the other two required stoma creation. Based on these domestic findings, TAI has been covered by insurance since 2018 under the category of “Home Transanal Self-Irrigation Guidance and Management Fee”. However, all three patients in whom colonic perforation occurred had a history of surgery for either rectal cancer or rectal prolapse. Thus, patients with a history of rectal surgery were not eligible for insurance coverage. From 2020, it has become possible to calculate the “surcharge for materials for home transanal self-irrigation”. However, as of April 2023, TAI is still covered by insurance only for “patients with bowel defecation disorders caused by spinal cord injury who do not improve adequately with conservative treatment for more than 3 months (excluding patients who underwent rectal surgery).” In contrast, TAI is also performed overseas for LARS. In an observational study involving 26 patients with LARS, 21 patients (81%) continued the use of TAI, of whom 15 (71%) had complete resolution of FI[ ]. In addition, in a prospective observational study of 14 patients with LARS, the median frequency of defecation significantly decreased both during the daytime (from eight times to once a day) and the nighttime (from three times to none in a day), the CCFIS significantly improved from 17 to 5, and QoL also significantly improved during a median follow-up period of 29 months[ ]. Recently, a cone catheter with a conical tip was developed to enhance the safety of TAI for patients with defecation disorders after rectal surgery, including those with LARS, and was approved in Japan in 2020. The cone catheter does not have a balloon attached. Thus, it is necessary to hold the catheter in place during the infusion of irrigation fluid. However, it can prevent bowel injury associated with balloon inflation, and the catheter tip is designed to extend the upper border of the anal canal slightly. Thus, there is a lower risk of bowel injury caused by the catheter tip[ ]. A multicenter RCT has been conducted to compare the efficacy and safety of TAI using a cone catheter against standard treatment for LARS. The results showed that the LARS score (21.3 for TAI vs. 32.2 for standard treatment), major LARS rate (33% vs. 67%), and patient satisfaction scores (8.6 vs. 6.7) after 3 months were significantly better in the TAI group

Tibial nerve stimulation Statement • The evidence for the efficacy of tibial nerve stimulation (TNS) is low, and currently, it cannot be considered effective for fecal incontinence. Because it has not been approved in Japan, it is limited to use within the framework of clinical research. Abstract TNS is a treatment to improve fecal incontinence (FI) using an external nerve stimulator to electrically stimulate the tibial nerve, which runs behind the ankle medial malleolus. There are two methods: percutaneous TNS (PTNS), which involves the insertion of a needle electrode through the skin, and transcutaneous TNS (TTNS), which uses the adhesive of an electrode pad on the skin. Compared with sacral neuromodulation, TNS is less invasive, more cost-effective, and associated with fewer adverse events; however, TNS should only be performed within the framework of clinical research. Because the evidence for its efficacy is low, no dedicated medical device is available in Japan, and it is not covered by insurance. Commentary TNS can improve FI by electrically stimulating the sacral nerve plexus, similar to sacral neuromodulation, as the tibial nerve originates from the sacral nerve[ ]. TNS is less invasive, cost-effective, and associated with fewer adverse events than sacral neuromodulation. However, its effectiveness in improving FI has not yet been conclusively determined. This is because the therapy's optimal stimulation conditions and methods are unknown and have not been standardized. A systematic review[ ] of TNS identified six studies on PTNS, five studies on TTNS, and one study that examined both methods. Of these studies, 10 were case studies, and the remaining 2 were RCTs. Anal electrical stimulation Statement • Anal electrical stimulation (AES) is not considered helpful for fecal incontinence when used alone; however, it may be beneficial when combined with anal electromyographic biofeedback therapy. Nevertheless, it is limited to use within the framework of clinical research, as it has not been approved in Japan. Abstract AES is a treatment that improves fecal incontinence (FI) by electrically stimulating the anal canal with a stimulation electrode inserted in it. The target patients benefiting from this therapy are unknown, and the evidence supporting its efficacy is low. This therapy should only be performed within the framework of clinical research, as there is no dedicated stimulation electrode or stimulator commercially available in Japan, and it is not covered by insurance. That said, an RCT reported that the FI score was significantly improved when amplitude-modulated medium-frequency anal electrical stimulation was combined with anal electromyographic biofeedback therapy compared with either AES alone or biofeedback therapy alone. Thus, this finding highlights a promising area for future research. Commentary The mechanism by which AES improves FI is believed to involve stimulating the neuromuscular junction of the anal sphincter muscles, which passively contracts the anal sphincters, thereby enhancing their contraction strength[ , ]. Generally, in voluntary contraction exercises, such as pelvic floor muscle training or biofeedback (BF) therapy, thin slow-twitch muscle fibers (type I fibers) are activated, and thick fast-twitch muscle fibers (type II fibers) are gradually recruited as the exercise load increases[ ]. Therefore, an exercise intensity of ≥50% maximal muscle strength is required to activate fast-twitch muscles. In contrast, therapeutic electrical stimulation preferentially activates fast-twitch fibers because of their larger motor nerve axon diameters and lower electrical resistance; thus, it can effectively strengthen fast-twitch fibers crucial for maximum muscle strength[ , ]. Therefore, by combining voluntary contraction training and passive contraction using electrical stimulation, slow- and fast-twitch fibers can be strengthened in a well-balanced manner. As a result, AES for FI is often performed along with BF therapy and other pelvic floor physiotherapy methods[ , ]. In an RCT involving 40 patients with FI caused by obstetric trauma, the combination group receiving AES and anal electromyographic BF (EMG-BF) had significantly more patients who had been healed or improved than those in the BF alone group using a vaginal manometer[ ]. The fact that the effect was obtained even with 1 Hz, which does not induce muscle contraction, suggested that the contraction of the anal sphincters is not necessarily required for the effect to be manifested and that physical stimulation of the anal region and improved sensation may be involved[ ]. While the efficacy of AES alone has been reported in several case series[ - ], different stimulation electrodes and devices, as well as current intensity, frequency, pulse width, and energization time have not been standardized. Consequently, the 2007 Cochrane review concluded that although AES may be effective for FI, the available data were insufficient to draw reliable conclusions regarding its effectiveness[ ]. However, low-frequency stimulation stimulates nociceptors in the skin and mucous membranes, causing pain when the current is increased[ , ]. However, they are not currently available for sale in Japan. Abstract Anal insert device is a treatment modality to prevent fecal incontinence (FI), in which a dedicated device is plugged into the anus and retained in the rectum to block the anal canal. Patients with normal rectal sensitivity or rectal hypersensitivity often cannot tolerate the discomfort caused by the retention of the device in the anorectum; thus, this treatment is considered suitable for older individuals with diminished rectal sensation or patients with spinal cord injuries, as they are less likely to experience discomfort from the device. This treatment can also effectively prevent FI in patients with normal rectal sensitivity if they can continue using the anal insert device without experiencing any discomfort. Therefore, this treatment may be a valuable option for patients who have not responded to or are unsuitable for other conservative treatments. Currently, however, anal insert devices are not commercially available in Japan. Commentary Several shapes and materials of anal insertable devices have been developed and used[ , ]. The Peristeen Ⓡ Anal Plug (hereafter referred to as Anal Plug Ⓡ ) was previously sold in Japan[ ]; however, because of changes in European medical device regulations, its production was discontinued in June 2023. As a result, anal insertable devices are currently not commercially available in Japan. According to the latest systematic review on insertable devices for the treatment of FI, 11 studies that examined anal incontinence devices from 1991 to 2019 included six focused on the Coloplast ‘Tulip’ design (Anal Plug Ⓡ ), 2 on the Procon/ProTect device, and 3 on the Renew Ⓡ Insert[ ]. In a prospective study evaluating the efficacy of Anal Plug Ⓡ , 7 (23%) out of 30 patients with FI discontinued its use within 1 week because of discomfort. However, 23 (77%) continued its use for 3 weeks, among whom 21 (70%) requested further continued use[ ]. Abstract Vaginal insert device is a fecal incontinence (FI) treatment device for women for the prevention of FI. A dedicated device is inserted and placed in the vagina, and a balloon is inflated in the vagina to extramurally block the rectum just above the anal canal. The Eclipse System is one of the dedicated devices. However, in Japan, it is not commercially available, is neither approved nor covered by insurance, and thus is limited to use within the framework of clinical research. This device cannot be placed properly in 20%-30% of patients, but its treatment success rate after 1 year is approximately 70% in patients in whom the device can be placed properly without discomfort. Its main adverse events are vaginal mucosal injury and bleeding, urinary incontinence and urgency, and vaginal and pelvic discomfort, most of which are noticed during the trial insert period, and no serious adverse events have been reported. Commentary Vaginal insert device is a FI treatment device for women. In the treatment, a dedicated device is inserted and placed in the vagina, and a balloon is inflated in the vagina to extramurally block the rectum just above the anal canal for the prevention of FI. The Eclipse System (Pelvalon, USA) is one of the dedicated devices, but it has not been approved in Japan. The insertion part of the Eclipse System is called an insert, and a balloon is attached to the rectal side of the silicone-coated stainless-steel base. The balloon is inflated by a removable pressure-regulating pump to block the rectum anteriorly and extramurally. When patients want to defecate, they deflate the balloon by manipulating the pump on their own. This device can be used in patients who have undergone hysterectomy[ ] and is contraindicated in the presence of vaginal infection or an open wound. The same research group has reported three prospective multicenter cohort studies on the usefulness of this therapy[ - ]. In the first study by Richter et al.[ ], who have developed this system, 110 adult women with four or more episodes of FI in 2 weeks were fitted with the system, and the usefulness of this therapy could be evaluated in only 61 women (56%) because 49 women dropped out, including 32 (29%) in whom the system could not be properly placed in the vagina. Of the 61 women, 48 (78%) achieved treatment success with a reduction of ≥50% in FI frequency after 1 month of use, and 38 (62%) achieved treatment success after 3 months of use. The main adverse events in the 110 women fitted with this system were pelvic spasm/discomfort in 25 women (23%) and urinary incontinence/urgency in 13 women (12%), most of which were noticed during the trial insert period, and no serious adverse events have been reported. Surgical Treatment for Fecal Incontinence Standard surgical treatments for fecal incontinence (FI) include anal sphincteroplasty and sacral neuromodulation as the first-line surgical treatments and stoma construction as the second-line surgical treatment. In addition, special surgical treatments, such as antegrade continence enema (ACE), graciloplasty, and VR, are included in the flowchart but are only performed in a limited number of institutions. Other surgical treatments include biomaterial injection, which is currently not available in Japan but is performed overseas, and anal sphincter regenerative therapy, whose development is anticipated in the future. In contrast, artificial bowel sphincter, magnetic anal sphincter, and puborectal sling, which had been included in the first edition of these guidelines, are not included in this revised edition because they are no longer performed even overseas because of concerns about complications resulting from the implantation of artificial materials. The level of evidence for surgical treatment in treating FI is generally low, except for novel procedures, such as sacral neuromodulation, which has been covered by insurance in Japan since 2014. This is mainly because RCTs and large-scale clinical trials are difficult to conduct owing to the nature of the surgical treatments. Other factors contributing to the low level of evidence were the lack of standardized definitions for FI and fecal continence as well as the lack of standardized methods for evaluating the severity of FI in the past. However, currently, evaluation methods are becoming standardized, as many studies use “a reduction of ≥50% in FI frequency” as the definition of successful treatment and the FIQL as the FI-specific QoL evaluation scale, thereby improving the level of evidence for surgical treatment. Although the surgical treatment flowchart for FI has been modified over time, surgical treatment should be selected in order, starting with the most minimally invasive procedure, as FI is a benign condition. For these surgical treatments to be properly selected and performed in Japan, the characteristics of each treatment must be well known. This section provides an abstract and commentary covering each treatment. In addition, for FI caused by organic diseases or anatomical abnormalities, such as rectal prolapse, prolapsed internal hemorrhoids, and rectovaginal fistula, treating the underlying disease often improves FI. Thus, this section does not cover treatment for these conditions. A.

Anal sphincter repair/sphincteroplasty Statement • Anal sphincter repair/sphincteroplasty is proposed to be performed for the treatment of fecal incontinence caused by laceration of the anal sphincter resulting from childbirth trauma. The short-term outcomes are favorable, but the outcomes deteriorate in the long term. Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B Abstract The surgical techniques of anal sphincter repair/sphincteroplasty for third- and fourth-degree perineal lacerations include direct repair and overlapping sphincteroplasty, which have similar efficacy in the short term. Complications include wound infection, wound dehiscence, and rectovaginal fistula. In the long term, the treatment effects often deteriorate, and in such cases, other treatments, such as drug therapy, biofeedback training, and sacral neuromodulation, are recommended rather than repeating anal sphincteroplasty. Commentary Anal sphincter repair/sphincteroplasty is a procedure that usually involves suturing lacerated anal sphincter tissue caused by vaginal trauma. Repair performed immediately after trauma is called anal sphincter repair, whereas repair performed later is called anal sphincteroplasty. There are two surgical techniques, namely direct repair, which involves directly suturing anal sphincter edges, and overlapping sphincteroplasty, which involves suturing the superimposed anal sphincter and scar tissue together[ ]. Randomized clinical trials comparing these two techniques have reported similar efficacy[ ]. This surgical procedure is mainly indicated for third- and fourth-degree perineal lacerations resulting from childbirth. Occasionally, this procedure is performed after anal fistula surgery or after traffic accidents, but there is a lack of evidence on its efficacy in these cases. The short-term efficacy for childbirth-induced trauma has been reported to be 60%-85%[ , ]. One study in Japan reported significant improvement in CCFIS and maximum squeeze pressure at 3 months after surgery compared with before surgery[ ]. Complications include wound infection, which can lead to wound dehiscence and may also lead to rectovaginal fistulas[ ]. Prognostic predictors of failure of anal sphincteroplasty include pudendal neuropathy, history of anal sphincteroplasty, advanced age, and impaired rectal sensation[ ]. In high-risk patients, the possibility that the surgical outcome may not be as expected should be fully explained, and informed consent should be obtained. Although anal sphincteroplasty for childbirth trauma has favorable short-term outcomes, as described above, the efficacy of treatment has been reported to decline to 10%-14% in the long term[ , - ]. Reasons for this include atrophy of the anal sphincter tissue caused by degeneration of the anal sphincter due to aging, tissue extension, and decreased pudendal nerve function. One study showed that repeat anal sphincteroplasty is effective in 50% of patients[ ]; however, because of the small number of cases and a lack of other reports, repeat anal sphincteroplasty is generally not recommended. In addition, in patients in whom several decades have passed since the trauma, it is difficult to obtain desired outcomes from anal sphincteroplasty because of aging. Therefore, initial drug therapy and other conservative treatments, such as biofeedback training, should be offered first. If no improvement is observed, sacral neuromodulation is recommended[ ]. CQ2. When is the best time to refer patients with fecal incontinence after delivery to a specialized facility? Strength of Recommendation: Weak (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C Commentary There is a paucity of literature describing the timing of consultation and referral to specialist facilities for postpartum fecal incontinence (FI). This issue has been addressed in reports from clinics specializing in postpartum pelvic floor disorders[ , ] and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists guidelines for the management of third- and fourth-degree perineal lacerations (anal sphincter injuries)[ ] ( ). OASIS is an important risk factor for FI after vaginal delivery, and if they are not diagnosed and treated as needed, FI can lead to a lifelong decline in QOL[ ]. In particular, if a severe perineal wound dehiscence or a large amount of fecal discharge from the vagina is observed immediately after anal sphincter repair for OASIS, the repair may be inadequate, and early re-repair is desirable. Thus, we propose an immediate referral to a specialized facility where surgical treatment is available. In addition, even if the condition is not severe enough that no severe perineal wound dehiscence or fecal discharge in a large amount from the vagina is observed, if FI, rectovaginal or recto-perineal fistula, or delayed perineal wound healing caused by OASIS is suspected, we propose an immediate referral to a specialized facility where surgical treatment can be performed, within reasonable limits. According to a report by Wan et al.[ ] on the performance of a perineal clinic (a clinic specializing in postpartum pelvic floor disorders), of 3,254 first-time patients, 1,892 (58.1%) had OASIS and 765 (23.5%) had perineal wound complications. In addition, they reported that patients with OASIS of grade 3b or higher, with injury extending to more than 50% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter, had a higher incidence of FI, lower anal pressure, persistent anal sphincter defects on endoanal ultrasonography, a higher incidence of fistula formation, and a higher need for anal sphincter re-suturing. Furthermore, Johannessen et al.[ ] reported that OASIS extending to the internal anal sphincter (3c) or to the anal epithelium (grade 4) was associated with a higher risk of developing FI than OASIS extending to the external anal sphincter (3b or lower). Sultan and Thakar[ ] reported that patients with grade 3 or 4 OASIS at a high risk of developing FI should pay attention to signs of wound infection and dehiscence, such as increased pain, anal bleeding, and purulent discharge from the wound, during the first 6-8 weeks postpartum. Moreover, Jibrel et al.[ ] reported from a facility specializing in postpartum patients that the average timing of first visit in 1,138 patients was 64 days (26-160 days) postpartum, and surgery was performed in 103 patients (9.1%) within 1 year after the first visit. Of the patients indicated for surgery, 53 (51.5%) underwent it for FI, and in terms of surgical procedure, 39 (37.9%) underwent anal sphincteroplasty for OASIS, 34 (33.0%) underwent perineal laceration re-suturing, and 20 (19.4%) underwent rectovaginal fistula repair, with an average of 153 days (79-282 days) from delivery to surgery. In conclusion, wound management in obstetrics should be prioritized within the first 2 months after vaginal delivery because of the high incidence of complications associated with the wound healing process. However, at the same time, considering the need for subsequent surgical treatment for OASIS, if FI, rectovaginal or recto-perineal fistula, or delayed perineal wound healing caused by OASIS is suspected, we propose an immediate referral to a specialized facility where surgical treatment can be performed, within reasonable limits. Johannessen et al. prospectively studied the course of anal incontinence, including gas incontinence, after delivery in 1,571 primiparas at the end of pregnancy as well as at 6 months, 1 year, and 6 years postpartum and noted that 65% of the women had natural vaginal delivery, 20% had abnormal vaginal delivery, such as vacuum forceps delivery and delivery complicated by OASIS, and 15% underwent cesarean section. The prevalence of anal incontinence after delivery was highest in patients who had undergone instrumental delivery, followed by normal vaginal delivery and cesarean section. However, the incidence of anal incontinence immediately after delivery was approximately 20% regardless of the mode of delivery. In addition, regardless of the mode of delivery, anal incontinence improved and the prevalence decreased up to 1 year postpartum. However, the prevalence of anal incontinence at 6 years was highest in patients who had undergone instrumental delivery (23%) compared with those who had undergone normal vaginal delivery (12%) or cesarean section (8%). The guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists[ ] recommends that patients who have undergone anal sphincter repair for OASIS be informed that 60%-80% of patients are asymptomatic with respect to anal incontinence after 1 year. In conclusion, FI in the absence of clinical evidence of OASIS, rectovaginal or recto-perineal fistula, or delayed perineal wound healing can

However, the prevalence of anal incontinence at 6 years was highest in patients who had undergone instrumental delivery (23%) compared with those who had undergone normal vaginal delivery (12%) or cesarean section (8%). The guideline published by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists[ ] recommends that patients who have undergone anal sphincter repair for OASIS be informed that 60%-80% of patients are asymptomatic with respect to anal incontinence after 1 year. In contrast, if FI persists 1 year after delivery, it may be due to clinically undiagnosed OASIS or may require treatment regardless of the cause. According to a meta-analysis of studies evaluating the relationship between anal incontinence and the diagnosis of OASIS by ultrasonography (103 studies, 16,110 patients)[ ], among women after vaginal delivery, 26% were diagnosed with OASIS by ultrasonography and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 19%. In addition, in 3,688 women with clinically unsuspected OASIS, 13% were diagnosed with OASIS by ultrasonography, and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 14%. Furthermore, of 7,549 patients who underwent anal sphincter repair for OASIS, 55% had residual anal sphincter defects on ultrasonography, and the prevalence of anal incontinence was 38%. The prevalence of anal incontinence was significantly (3.74 times) higher in patients diagnosed with OASIS than in those in whom OASIS was not observed on ultrasonography. Thus, this meta-analysis demonstrated the importance of diagnosing the presence or absence of OASIS by ultrasonography, even if OASIS is not clinically detected. Moreover, Wan et al.[ ] performed endoanal ultrasonography on 134 patients with anal incontinence despite no clinical diagnosis of OASIS and found OASIS in 40 patients (30%). Of the 134 patients, 25 (19%) received biofeedback therapy, 6 (4.5%) anal sphincteroplasty, and 1 (0.7%) sacral neuromodulation. In conclusion, if FI persists 1 year after delivery, it may be due to clinically undiagnosed OASIS. Thus, we propose referral to a specialized facility where endoanal ultrasonography is available. At specialized facilities, FI can be expected to improve with specialized treatments, such as biofeedback therapy, anal sphincteroplasty, and sacral neuromodulation, depending on the cause and severity of the FI. CQ3. Which mode of delivery is recommended for pregnant women with a history of obstetric anal sphincter injury: vaginal delivery or cesarean section? Statement • If a patient has a history of anal obstetric anal sphincter injury, it is recommended that pregnant women have a consultation with a specialist regarding the next mode of delivery if they want. Strength of Recommendation: Strong, (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: C • If a pregnant woman with a history of obstetric anal sphincter injury during childbirth has no symptoms of fecal incontinence before her next delivery or no obvious abnormalities on endoanal ultrasonography or anal manometry, it is proposed that she consider a vaginal delivery. Strength of Recommendation: Weak, (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B • If a pregnant woman with a history of anal obstetric anal sphincter injury during childbirth has mild symptoms of fecal incontinence before her next delivery, it is proposed that she undergo endoanal ultrasonography and anal manometry if possible, and consider a planned cesarean section if obvious abnormalities are found to avoid worsening of fecal incontinence. Strength of Recommendation: Weak, (Consensus Rate: 100%), Level of Evidence: B • If a pregnant woman with a history of obstetric anal sphincter injury during childbirth has severe symptoms of fecal incontinence before the next delivery, it is proposed that she consider a vaginal delivery because it is unlikely that the fecal incontinence will be further aggravated by a vaginal delivery.
